**Livorno** (Italian: [[liˈvorno]](./Help:IPA/Italian "Help:IPA/Italian") [ⓘ](/wiki/File:It-Livorno.ogg "File:It-Livorno.ogg")) is a port city on the [Ligurian Sea](./Ligurian_Sea "Ligurian Sea")[[2]](./Livorno#cite_note-2) on the western coast of the [Tuscany](./Tuscany "Tuscany") region of [Italy](./Italy "Italy").[[3]](./Livorno#cite_note-3) It is the capital of the [Province of Livorno](./Province_of_Livorno "Province of Livorno"), having a population of 152,916 residents as of 2025.[[1]](./Livorno#cite_note-population-1) It is traditionally known in English as **Leghorn** (pronounced [/lɛˈɡɔːrn/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [*leg-ORN*](./Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"),[[4]](./Livorno#cite_note-Cham20-4)[[5]](./Livorno#cite_note-collins-concise-5) [/ˈlɛɡhɔːrn/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [*LEG-horn*](./Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")[[6]](./Livorno#cite_note-oxf-6) or [/ˈlɛɡərn/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [*LEG-ərn*](./Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")).[[7]](./Livorno#cite_note-7)[[8]](./Livorno#cite_note-8)

During the [Renaissance](./Italian_Renaissance "Italian Renaissance"), Livorno was designed as an "[ideal town](./Ideal_town "Ideal town")". Developing considerably from the second half of the [16th century](./16th_century "16th century") by the will of the [House of Medici](./House_of_Medici "House of Medici"), Livorno was an important [free port](./Free_port "Free port"). Its intense commercial activity was largely dominated by foreign traders. Also the seat of consulates and shipping companies, it became the main port-city of the [Grand Duchy of Tuscany](./Grand_Duchy_of_Tuscany "Grand Duchy of Tuscany").[[9]](./Livorno#cite_note-9) The high status of a multiethnic and multicultural Livorno lasted until the second half of the nineteenth century, when it was surpassed by other cities. Evidence of that prosperous time can be seen in the many churches, villas, and palaces of the city.[[10]](./Livorno#cite_note-treccanilivorno-10)

Livorno is considered to be the most modern among all the Tuscan cities, and is the third most-populous of the region, after [Florence](./Florence "Florence") and [Prato](./Prato "Prato").[[11]](./Livorno#cite_note-11)[[12]](./Livorno#cite_note-12)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/83/Livorno_map_17th_Century.jpg/500px-Livorno_map_17th_Century.jpg)](./File:Livorno_map_17th_Century.jpg)

Fortifications of Livorno in the 17th century

### Origins

The origins of Livorno are controversial, although the place was inhabited since the [Neolithic](./Neolithic "Neolithic") Age. This is documented by the worked bones, and pieces of copper and ceramic found on the [Livorno Hills](./Livorno_Hills "Livorno Hills") in a cave between Ardenza and Montenero. The [Etruscan](./Etruscan_cities "Etruscan cities") settlement was called Labro.[[13]](./Livorno#cite_note-13)

The construction of the [Via Aurelia](./Via_Aurelia "Via Aurelia") coincided with the occupation of the region by the [Romans](./Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome"). They are also known for their [toponyms](./Toponymy "Toponymy") and the ruins of towers. The natural cove called Liburna is a reference to the type of ship, the [liburna](./Liburna "Liburna"), adopted by [Roman navy](./Roman_navy "Roman navy") from the [Liburnians](./Liburnians "Liburnians"). Other ancient toponyms include *Salviano* (Salvius) and *Antignano* (Ante ignem), which was the place situated before *Ardenza* (Ardentia), where beacons directed the ships to [Porto Pisano](./Porto_Pisano "Porto Pisano"). [Cicero](./Cicero "Cicero") mentioned Liburna in a letter to his brother, in which he called it [Labrone](./Labrone?action=edit&redlink=1 "Labrone").[[14]](./Livorno#cite_note-14)

### Medieval

Livorna is mentioned for the first time in 1017 as a small coastal village, the port and the remains of a Roman tower under the rule of [Lucca](./Lucca "Lucca"). In 1077, a tower was built by [Matilda of Tuscany](./Matilda_of_Tuscany "Matilda of Tuscany"). The [Republic of Pisa](./Republic_of_Pisa "Republic of Pisa") owned Livorna from 1103 and built a quadrangular fort called *Quadratura dei Pisani* ("Quarter of the Pisans") to defend the port.[[10]](./Livorno#cite_note-treccanilivorno-10) *Porto Pisano* was destroyed after the crushing defeat of the Pisan fleet in the [Battle of Meloria](./Battle_of_Meloria_(1284) "Battle of Meloria (1284)") in 1284.[[15]](./Livorno#cite_note-15)

In 1399, Pisa sold Livorna to the [Visconti of Milan](./Visconti_of_Milan "Visconti of Milan"); in 1405 it was sold to the [Republic of Genoa](./Republic_of_Genoa "Republic of Genoa"); and on 28 August 1421 it was bought by the [Republic of Florence](./Republic_of_Florence "Republic of Florence").[[10]](./Livorno#cite_note-treccanilivorno-10) The name 'Leghorn' was derived from the [Genoese](./Genoese_dialect "Genoese dialect") name Ligorna.[[16]](./Livorno#cite_note-Ciccone-16) *Livorno* was used certainly in the eighteenth century by Florentines.[[16]](./Livorno#cite_note-Ciccone-16)

Between 1427 and 1429, a census counted 118 families in Livorno, including 423 persons. Monks, Jews, military personnel, and the homeless were not included in the census.[[17]](./Livorno#cite_note-17) The only remainder of medieval Livorno is a fragment of two towers and a wall, located inside the [Fortezza Vecchia](./Livorno#Fortezza_Vecchia).

### Medicean period (1500–1650)

After the arrival of the [Medici](./House_of_Medici "House of Medici"), the ruling dynasty of Florence, some modifications were made in the city. Between 1518 and 1534 the *[Fortezza Vecchia](./Old_Fortress,_Livorno "Old Fortress, Livorno")* was constructed, and the voluntary resettlement of the population to Livorno was stimulated. Livorno still remained a rather insignificant coastal fortress.[[18]](./Livorno#cite_note-18) By 1551, the population had grown to 1562 residents.[[10]](./Livorno#cite_note-treccanilivorno-10)

Seat of the crusading and corsairing [Order of Saint Stephen](./Order_of_Saint_Stephen "Order of Saint Stephen") after 1561, distinctive for its aggressive approach towards the Muslim world, Livorno became a major Mediterranean [slave trade](./History_of_slavery "History of slavery") hub in the early modern period, rivalling Malta's.[[19]](./Livorno#cite_note-19) Its share of slave population may have been over a 25% of the population.[[20]](./Livorno#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavis2018873-20)

During the [Italian Renaissance](./Italian_Renaissance "Italian Renaissance"), when the settlement was ruled by the [Grand Duchy of Tuscany](./Grand_Duchy_of_Tuscany "Grand Duchy of Tuscany") of the [House of Medici](./House_of_Medici "House of Medici"), Livorno was designed as an "[Ideal town](./Ideal_town "Ideal town")".[[10]](./Livorno#cite_note-treccanilivorno-10) In 1577 the architect [Bernardo Buontalenti](./Bernardo_Buontalenti "Bernardo Buontalenti") drew up the first plan.[[10]](./Livorno#cite_note-treccanilivorno-10) The new fortified town had a [pentagonal](./Pentagonal "Pentagonal") design, for which it is called *[Pentagono del Buontalenti](./Livorno#Pentagono_del_Buontalenti)*, incorporating the original settlement. The *[Porto Mediceo](./Port_of_Livorno#Porto_Mediceo "Port of Livorno")* was overlooked and defended by [towers](./Tower "Tower") and fortresses leading to the [town centre](./Town_centre "Town centre").

In the late 1580s, [Ferdinando I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany](./Ferdinando_I_de'_Medici,_Grand_Duke_of_Tuscany "Ferdinando I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany"), declared Livorno a [free port](./List_of_free_ports "List of free ports") (*porto franco*), which meant that the goods traded here were [duty-free](./Duty-free_shop "Duty-free shop") within the area of the town's control.

In 1593, the Duke's administration established the *Leggi Livornine* to regulate trade.[[10]](./Livorno#cite_note-treccanilivorno-10) These laws protected merchant activities from crime and [racketeering](./Racket_(crime) "Racket (crime)"), and instituted laws regarding [international trade](./International_trade "International trade"). The laws established a well-regulated market and were in force until 1603. Also expanding Christian tolerance, the laws offered the right of public [freedom of religion](./Freedom_of_religion "Freedom of religion") and [amnesty](./Amnesty "Amnesty") to people having to gain [penance](./Penance "Penance") from clergy in order to conduct civil business. The Grand Duke attracted numerous Turks, Persians, Moors, Greeks, and Armenians, along with [Jewish](./Jews "Jews") immigrants. Sephardic Jews began to immigrate to Livorno in the late sixteenth century, following the [Alhambra Decree](./Alhambra_Decree "Alhambra Decree") and expulsion of Jews from Spain and Portugal. Livorno extended rights and privileges to them, and they contributed greatly to the mercantile wealth and scholarship in the city.

Livorno became an enlightened European city and one of the most important ports of the entire [Mediterranean Basin](./Mediterranean_Basin "Mediterranean Basin"). Many European [foreigners](./Alien_(law) "Alien (law)") moved to Livorno. These included Christian Protestant reformers who supported such leaders as [Martin Luther](./Martin_Luther "Martin Luther"), [John Calvin](./John_Calvin "John Calvin"), and others. [French](./French_people "French people"), [Dutch](./Dutch_people "Dutch people"), and English arrived, along with Orthodox [Greeks](./Greeks "Greeks"). Meanwhile, Jews continued to trade under their previous treaties with the Grand Duke. On 19 March 1606, Ferdinando I de' Medici elevated Livorno to the rank of city; the ceremony was held in the *Fortezza Vecchia* Chapel of [Francis of Assisi](./Francis_of_Assisi "Francis of Assisi").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/Chiesa_Santa_Caterina%2C_Livorno.jpg/250px-Chiesa_Santa_Caterina%2C_Livorno.jpg)](./File:Chiesa_Santa_Caterina,_Livorno.jpg)

[Santa Caterina, Livorno](./Santa_Caterina_(Livorno) "Santa Caterina (Livorno)")

The [Counter-Reformation](./Counter-Reformation "Counter-Reformation") increased tensions among Christians; dissidents to the [Papacy](./Pope "Pope") were targeted by various Catholic absolute rulers. Livorno's tolerance declined during the [European wars of religion](./European_wars_of_religion "European wars of religion"). But, in the preceding period, the merchants of Livorno had developed a series of trading networks with Protestant Europe, and the Dutch, British, and Germans worked to retain these. In 1653 a naval battle, the [Battle of Leghorn](./Battle_of_Leghorn "Battle of Leghorn"), was fought near Livorno during the [First Anglo-Dutch War](./First_Anglo-Dutch_War "First Anglo-Dutch War").

### 17th century and later

At the end of the 17th century, Livorno underwent a period of great [urban planning](./Urban_planning "Urban planning") and expansion. Near the defensive pile of the Old Fortress, a new fortress was built, together with the town walls and the system of navigable canals through neighbourhoods. After the port of [Pisa](./Pisa "Pisa") had silted up in the 13th century, its distance from the sea increased and it lost its dominance in trade. Livorno took over as the main port in [Tuscany](./Tuscany "Tuscany"). By 1745 Livorno's population had risen to 32,534.[[10]](./Livorno#cite_note-treccanilivorno-10)

The more successful of the European powers re-established trading houses in the region, especially the British with the [Levant Company](./Levant_Company "Levant Company"). In turn, the trading networks grew, and with those, Britain's cultural contact with Tuscany. An increasing number of British writers, artists, philosophers, and travellers visited the area and developed the unique historical ties between the two communities. The British referred to the city in English as "Leghorn", derived from the Genoese term. Through the centuries, the city's trade fortunes fell and rose according to the success or failure of the Great Powers. The British and their Protestant allies were important to its trade.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/52/Livorno_map_of_the_town_%281849%29_by_Guesdon_01.jpg/330px-Livorno_map_of_the_town_%281849%29_by_Guesdon_01.jpg)](./File:Livorno_map_of_the_town_(1849)_by_Guesdon_01.jpg)

Bird's-eye view of Livorno in the mid 19th century.

During the [Italian campaigns of the French Revolutionary Wars](./Italian_campaigns_of_the_French_Revolutionary_Wars "Italian campaigns of the French Revolutionary Wars") of the late eighteenth century, Napoleon's troops occupied Livorno along with the rest of Tuscany. Under the [Continental System](./Continental_System "Continental System"), the French prohibited trade with Britain, and the economy of Livorno suffered greatly. The French had altogether taken over Tuscany by 1808, incorporating it into the Napoleonic empire. After the [Congress of Vienna](./Congress_of_Vienna "Congress of Vienna"), Austrian rule replaced the French.

In 1861, [Italy](./Italy "Italy") succeeded in its [wars of unification](./Unification_of_Italy "Unification of Italy"). At that time the city counted 96,471 inhabitants.[[10]](./Livorno#cite_note-treccanilivorno-10) Livorno and [Tuscany](./Tuscany "Tuscany") became part of the new [Kingdom of Italy](./Kingdom_of_Italy "Kingdom of Italy") and, as part of the Kingdom, the town lost its status as a free port. The city's commercial importance declined.

In the 18th and 19th centuries, Livorno had numerous [public parks](./Urban_park "Urban park") housing important museums such as the *[Museo Civico Giovanni Fattori](./Livorno#Museo_Civico_"Giovanni_Fattori")*, *[Museo di storia naturale del Mediterraneo](./Livorno#Museo_di_storia_naturale_del_Mediterraneo)*, and [cultural institutions](./Cultural_institution "Cultural institution") as the *[Biblioteca Labronica F.D. Guerrazzi](./Livorno#Biblioteca_Labronica)* and others in [Neoclassical style](./Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") as *[Cisternone](./Cisternoni_of_Livorno#La_Gran_Conserva "Cisternoni of Livorno")*, *Teatro Goldoni* and [Liberty style](./Liberty_style "Liberty style") as *Palazzo Corallo*, *[Mercato](./Market_(place) "Market (place)") delle Vettovaglie*, *[Stabilimento termale Acque](./Thermae "Thermae") della Salute*, the *[Scuole elementari](./Primary_education#Italy "Primary education") Benci* all the last on project by Angiolo Badaloni.

In the early 19th century, the American [Elizabeth Ann Seton](./Elizabeth_Ann_Seton "Elizabeth Ann Seton") converted from Protestantism to Catholicism while visiting Italian friends in Livorno. She later was canonized as the first American-born saint.

During the 1930s, numerous [villas](./Villa "Villa") were built on the avenue along the sea in [Liberty style](./Art_Nouveau "Art Nouveau") based on designs by Cioni.[[21]](./Livorno#cite_note-21) These added to the architectural richness of the city.

Livorno suffered extensive damage during [World War II](./World_War_II "World War II"). Many historic sites and buildings were destroyed by bombs of the [Allies](./Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of World War II") preceding their invasion of Italy, including the [cathedral](./Livorno#Cathedral_of_Saint_Francis_of_Assisi) and [Synagogue of Livorno](./Synagogue_of_Livorno "Synagogue of Livorno").

Since the late 20th century, Livorno's residents have become well known for their [left-wing politics](./Left-wing_politics "Left-wing politics"). The [Italian Communist Party](./Italian_Communist_Party "Italian Communist Party") was founded in Livorno in 1921.

Climate
-------

Livorno has a hot-summer [mediterranean climate](./Mediterranean_climate "Mediterranean climate") ([Köppen climate classification](./Köppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification") *Csa*). Summers have warm days with the heat lingering on throughout the night, hence going above the [subtropical](./Subtropical_climate "Subtropical climate") threshold in spite of its relatively high latitude. Winters are mild for the latitude due to the moderating influence from the [Mediterranean Sea](./Mediterranean_Sea "Mediterranean Sea"). Precipitation is in a wet winter/dry summer pattern as with all climates fitting the Mediterranean definition.

Further information: [2017 Livorno floods](./2017_Livorno_floods "2017 Livorno floods")

#### Armenian community

See also: [Sceriman family](./Sceriman_family "Sceriman family")

[Ferdinando I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany](./Ferdinando_I_de'_Medici,_Grand_Duke_of_Tuscany "Ferdinando I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany") issued in 1591 a decree encouraging [Armenians](./Armenians "Armenians") to settle in Livorno to increase its trade with the Ottoman Empire and western Asia. By the beginning of the 17th century, Armenians operated 120 shops in town.[[25]](./Livorno#cite_note-25) In 1701 the Armenian community, who were members of the [Armenian Apostolic Church](./Armenian_Apostolic_Church "Armenian Apostolic Church"), were authorized to build their own church, which they dedicated to [Gregory the Illuminator](./Gregory_the_Illuminator "Gregory the Illuminator"). The project was by [Giovanni Battista Foggini](./Giovanni_Battista_Foggini "Giovanni Battista Foggini") and the church was completed a few years later but did not open for worship until 1714.[[26]](./Livorno#cite_note-26) The church had a Latin cross plan and a dome at the intersection of the transept and nave. Destroyed during World War II, it was partly restored in 2008 but is not open to worship.

#### Greek community

The first [Greeks](./Greeks "Greeks") who settled in Livorno early in the 16th century were former mercenaries in the fleet of [Cosimo de' Medici](./Cosimo_de'_Medici "Cosimo de' Medici") and their descendants. This community grew and became significant in the 18th and 19th centuries when Livorno became one of the principal hubs of the Mediterranean trade.[[27]](./Livorno#cite_note-27) Most of the new Greek immigrants came from western Greece, [Chios](./Chios "Chios"), [Epirus](./Epirus "Epirus") and [Cappadocia](./Cappadocian_Greeks "Cappadocian Greeks").

Based on its status since the late 16th century as a [free port](./List_of_free_ports "List of free ports") (*port franc*) and the warehouses constructed for long-term storage of goods and grains from the [Levant](./Levant "Levant"), until the late 19th century Livorno enjoyed a strong strategic position related to Greek mercantile interests in the [Black Sea](./Black_Sea "Black Sea"), the [Mediterranean Sea](./Mediterranean_Sea "Mediterranean Sea"), and the North Atlantic. The conflicts between Great Britain and France during the [Napoleonic Wars](./Napoleonic_Wars "Napoleonic Wars") of the early 19th century, with associated port embargoes, piracy, and confiscation of cargoes, played out to the advantage of those Greek merchants willing to accept risk. By the 1820s, Greek entrepreneurs gradually replaced the Protestant British, Dutch, French and other merchants who left the city.

The Greeks concentrated on the grain market, banking and ship-brokering. Cargoes of wheat from the Black Sea were received at Livorno, before being re-shipped to England. Returning ships carried textiles and other industrial goods, which Greek merchants shipped to [Alexandria](./Alexandria "Alexandria") and other destinations in the [Ottoman Empire](./Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire"). Chians controlled much of the trade. In 1839 Livorno had ten major commercial houses, led primarily by ethnic Greeks and Jewish Italians.[[28]](./Livorno#cite_note-28)

The ethnic Greek community (*nazione*) had a distinctive cultural and social identity based on their common [Greek Orthodox religion](./Greek_Orthodox_Church "Greek Orthodox Church"), language and history. In 1775 they established the Confraternity of Holy Trinity (*Confraternita della SS. Trinità*) and the [Church of the Santissima Trinità, Livorno](./Church_of_the_Santissima_Trinità,_Livorno?action=edit&redlink=1 "Church of the Santissima Trinità, Livorno") [[it](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiesa%20greco-ortodossa%20della%20Santissima%20Trinità "it:Chiesa greco-ortodossa della Santissima Trinità")], the second non-Catholic church in Tuscany. The Armenians had earlier built their own Orthodox church.[[29]](./Livorno#cite_note-29) The community founded a Greek school, awarding scholarships for higher studies to young Greeks from the [Peloponnese](./Peloponnese "Peloponnese"), Epirus, Chios or [Smyrna](./Smyrna "Smyrna"). The community raised funds to support the [Greek War of Independence](./Greek_War_of_Independence "Greek War of Independence") of 1821, as well as various Greek communities in the Ottoman Empire and in Italy.

It also assisted non-Greeks. The [Rodocanachi](./Rodocanachi "Rodocanachi") family financed the "School of Mutual Education" established in Livorno by the pedagogist [Enrico Mayer](./Enrico_Mayer?action=edit&redlink=1 "Enrico Mayer") [[it](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrico%20Mayer "it:Enrico Mayer")]. The community contributed to founding a school for poor Catholic children. The local governing authorities recognized the contributions of distinguished members of the Greek community (e.g. members of the Papoudoff, [Maurogordatos](./Mavrocordatos_family "Mavrocordatos family"), Rodocanachi, [Tossizza](./Tositsas_family?action=edit&redlink=1 "Tositsas family") [[el](https://el.wikipedia.org/wiki/Οικογένεια%20Τοσίτσα "el:Οικογένεια Τοσίτσα")] and other families) and granted them titles of nobility. After unification and the founding of the [Kingdom of Italy](./Kingdom_of_Italy "Kingdom of Italy") in 1861, the Greek community in Livorno declined, as the privileges of the free port were rescinded.[[30]](./Livorno#cite_note-30)

### Dialects

Vernacolo

Livorno inhabitants speak a variant of the Italian [Tuscan dialect](./Tuscan_dialect "Tuscan dialect"), known as a *[vernacolo](./Vernacular "Vernacular")*. *[Il Vernacoliere](./Il_Vernacoliere "Il Vernacoliere")*, a satirical comic-style magazine printed chiefly in the Livornese dialect, was founded in 1982 and is now nationally distributed.[[31]](./Livorno#cite_note-Official_website_history-31)

Bagitto

The *[bagitto](./Judeo-Italian_languages#Dialects "Judeo-Italian languages")* was a Judæo-Italian regional dialect once used by the [Jewish community in Livorno](./History_of_the_Jews_in_Livorno "History of the Jews in Livorno"). It was a language based on Italian, developed with words coming from Tuscan, Spanish, Portuguese, [Hebrew](./Hebrew_language "Hebrew language") and [Yiddish](./Yiddish "Yiddish"); the presence of Portuguese and Spanish words is due to the origin of the first Jews who came to Livorno, having been expelled from the Iberian peninsula in the late 15th century.

### *Cantiere navale fratelli Orlando*

Since 1866 Livorno has been noted for its [Cantiere navale fratelli Orlando](./Cantiere_navale_fratelli_Orlando "Cantiere navale fratelli Orlando"). [Azimut](./Azimut_Yachts "Azimut Yachts")-[Benetti](./Benetti "Benetti") acquired the Cantiere navale fratelli Orlando, then of [Fincantieri](./Fincantieri "Fincantieri"), in 2003.

### Eni petrochemical

The [Eni](./Eni "Eni") plant produces [gasoline](./Gasoline "Gasoline"), [diesel fuel](./Diesel_fuel "Diesel fuel"), [fuel oil](./Fuel_oil "Fuel oil") and [lubricants](./Lubricant "Lubricant"). Livorno refinery was established in 1936 by [Azienda Nazionale Idrogenazione Combustibili](./Azienda_Nazionale_Idrogenazione_Combustibili "Azienda Nazionale Idrogenazione Combustibili") (ANIC) but the plant was completely destroyed during World War II. The plant was rebuilt thanks to an agreement between the ANIC and the [Standard Oil](./Standard_Oil "Standard Oil") forming the STANIC. The production of the new plant raised from 700,000 to 2 million tons in 1955; nowadays the capacity of refining is 84,000 [barrels](./Barrel_(unit)#Oil_barrel "Barrel (unit)") per day. The refinery, now property of [Eni](./Eni "Eni"), is linked to the *Darsena petroli* (Oil dock) and to [Florence](./Florence "Florence") depots by two pipelines.[[33]](./Livorno#cite_note-33)

### *WASS Submarine Systems*

Main article: [WASS Submarine Systems](./WASS_Submarine_Systems "WASS Submarine Systems")

The former WASS (previously [Whitehead Alenia Sistemi Subacquei](./Whitehead_Alenia_Sistemi_Subacquei "Whitehead Alenia Sistemi Subacquei")) plant is based in Livorno, produced heavy and light [torpedoes](./Torpedo "Torpedo"), anti-torpedo countermeasure systems for submarines and ships and sonar systems for underwater surveillance.[[34]](./Livorno#cite_note-34) The factory came about in 1924 when the [Whitehead Torpedo Works](./Whitehead_Torpedo_Works "Whitehead Torpedo Works") was purchased by Giuseppe Orlando, one of the owners of the *[Cantiere navale fratelli Orlando](./Cantiere_navale_fratelli_Orlando "Cantiere navale fratelli Orlando")* of Livorno. [Whitehead Moto Fides](./Whitehead_Moto_Fides "Whitehead Moto Fides") continued the production of torpedoes in a new plant which opened in 1977 and still operating, now owned by [Fincantieri](./Fincantieri "Fincantieri").

### *Financial district*

Another important role is played by the financial service, concentrated above all in via Cairoli, called the small city of Livorno, in which the headquarters of banks, financial institutions and insurance companies are concentrated, as well as the Post Office Building.

### *Tuaca*

*[Tuaca](./Tuaca "Tuaca")* liqueur was produced in Livorno until 2010; the famous distillery was closed and operations were brought to the United States by the new owners. [Galliano](./Galliano_(liqueur) "Galliano (liqueur)") is still made here and enjoyed by locals and tourists alike.

### *Acquario comunale "Diacinto Cestoni"*

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Livorno_Aquarium_Diacinto_Cestoni_01_%40chesi.JPG/250px-Livorno_Aquarium_Diacinto_Cestoni_01_%40chesi.JPG)](./File:Livorno_Aquarium_Diacinto_Cestoni_01_@chesi.JPG)

*Acquario comunale Diacinto Cestoni*

Livorno Aquarium, dedicated to [Diacinto Cestoni](./Diacinto_Cestoni "Diacinto Cestoni"), is the main in Tuscany. It is situated by *[Terrazza Mascagni](./Livorno#Terrazza_Mascagni)* on the seafront promenade. It was built on a project by Enrico Salvais and Luigi Pastore as a heliotherapy centre and was opened to the public on 20 June 1937. Destroyed during World War II was rebuilt in 1950;[[35]](./Livorno#cite_note-35) in 1999 underwent extensive reconstruction, on a plan by Studio Gregotti and works carried out by Opera Laboratori Fiorentini, was opened definitely on 31 July 2010.[[36]](./Livorno#cite_note-36)
On the ground floor, the exhibition includes: Diacinto Cestoni Room which consists of 12 exhibition tanks, Mediterranean Area, Indus-Pacific tank, Caribbean Sea, Ligurian coast, Tropical waters, Greek-Roman archaeological coastal area. Livorno Aquarium has 33 exhibition tanks containing 2000 animals of 300 different species.[[37]](./Livorno#cite_note-37)

### [Museo Civico Giovanni Fattori](./Museo_Civico_Giovanni_Fattori "Museo Civico Giovanni Fattori")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/96/Villa_mibelli%2C_sala_da_fumo%2C_detta_Sala_Moresca_00.jpg/250px-Villa_mibelli%2C_sala_da_fumo%2C_detta_Sala_Moresca_00.jpg)](./File:Villa_mibelli,_sala_da_fumo,_detta_Sala_Moresca_00.jpg)

Moresque room in the *Museo civico Giovanni Fattori*

Dedicated to painter [Giovanni Fattori](./Giovanni_Fattori "Giovanni Fattori"), the museum mainly featuring contemporary art from the 19th-century was inaugurated in 1994 and is placed inside *Villa Mimbelli*, an 18th-century construction surrounded by a vast park. The origin of the museum dates back to 1877 when the [Comune](./Comune "Comune") of Livorno founded a Civic Gallery where to collect all the artistic objects kept in several places around the town; in the same period was written the guideline of the gallery which hosted a collection of paintings of authors by Livorno.[[38]](./Livorno#cite_note-38)

### *Museo Ebraico "Yeshivà Marini"*

The Yeshivà Marini Museum is housed in a neoclassical building already place of worship as Marini Oratory since 1867; once was home of the Confraternity Malbish Arumin which was provided to help the city's poor.[[39]](./Livorno#cite_note-39) In the post-war period was utilized as a synagogue in the waiting for the construction of the new one. The museum has a collection of liturgical objects coming from the old Synagogue destroyed in World War II. The commerce practised by the Jews community increased the property of the synagogue allowing a varied religious heritage of Dutch, Florentine, Venetian, Roman and Northern African origin. The display regard the [Torah ark](./Torah_ark "Torah ark"), the [sefer Torah](./Sefer_Torah "Sefer Torah"), paintings, religious objects as the Oriental-style wooden *hekhal*; the oldest and most important pieces went lost.[[40]](./Livorno#cite_note-40)

### *Museo di storia naturale del Mediterraneo*

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/71/Livorno_Villa_Webb_Henderson_01.JPG/250px-Livorno_Villa_Webb_Henderson_01.JPG)](./File:Livorno_Villa_Webb_Henderson_01.JPG)

*Museo di storia naturale del Mediterraneo*

The origins of the museum date back to 1929 and part of the objects went destroyed by World War II. After the war, the museum was reopened inside the Livorno Aquarium and only in 1980 was transferred to Villa Henderson. The museum is divided in several halls regarding the Man, the Man in the Mediterranean context, the Invertebrates, the Sea, the Flight in Nature. Inside the museum is a Planetarium and an Auditorium.

### *Museo Mascagnano*

The *Museo Mascagnano* houses memorabilia, documents and operas by the great [composer](./Composer "Composer") [Pietro Mascagni](./Pietro_Mascagni "Pietro Mascagni"), who lived here. Every year some of his operas are traditionally played during the lyric music season, which is organized by the [Goldoni](./Goldoni "Goldoni") Theatre. Also the *[Terrazza Mascagni](./Livorno#Terrazza_Mascagni)* is situated on the boulevard on the seafront, is named in his honour.

### *Orto Botanico del Mediterraneo*

The *[Orto Botanico del Mediterraneo](./Orto_Botanico_del_Mediterraneo "Orto Botanico del Mediterraneo")* is a [botanical garden](./Botanical_garden "Botanical garden") located on the grounds of the *[Museo di storia naturale del Mediterraneo](./Livorno#Museo_di_storia_naturale_del_Mediterraneo)*.

### Civil architecture

#### *Venezia Nuova*

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Panorama_Venezia_Nuova%2C_Livorno.JPG/500px-Panorama_Venezia_Nuova%2C_Livorno.JPG)](./File:Panorama_Venezia_Nuova,_Livorno.JPG)

*Venezia Nuova*

[Ferdinando II de' Medici](./Ferdinando_II_de'_Medici,_Grand_Duke_of_Tuscany "Ferdinando II de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany") considered, in 1629, the opportunity to enlarge the town, on project by Giovanni Battista Santi, toward north in an area included among *[Fortezza Vecchia](./Livorno#Fortezza_Vecchia)* and *[Fortezza Nuova](./Livorno#Fortezza_Nuova)*, in order to give an adequate space to the maritime and commercial activities. There was the need to build a mercantile district, close to *[Porto Mediceo](./Port_of_Livorno#Porto_Mediceo "Port of Livorno")*, provided with houses and depots to store the merchandise and a system of canals to facilitate their transport. The new *[rione](./Rione "Rione")* (district), called *[Venezia Nuova](./Venezia_Nuova?action=edit&redlink=1 "Venezia Nuova") [[it](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venezia%20Nuova "it:Venezia Nuova")]*, was built in an area gained to the sea, intersected by canals and linked to the town with bridges, for this reason, Venetians skilled workers were recruited.[[41]](./Livorno#cite_note-41)

The *Chiesa di Sant'Anna*, dedicated to [Saint Anne](./Saint_Anne "Saint Anne"), was built in 1631 on the ground of the Arch confraternity of the Company of the Nativity;[[42]](./Livorno#cite_note-42) in the same year Giovanni Battista Santi died and the control of the project passed to Giovanni Francesco Cantagallina though the works slowed down due to the lack of funds.[[43]](./Livorno#cite_note-43)

A new impulse to the works was given in 1656 concerning the distribution of the spaces where to build other houses and stores; consequently arose the problem of the diverse oriented road scheme with respect to the axis of *Piazza d’Arme*, it was resolved by adopting a road plan perpendicular to the [Navicelli channel](./Navicelli_channel "Navicelli channel"). The paving of the roads and along the canals in *Venezia Nuova* was provided in 1668,[[44]](./Livorno#cite_note-44) while the *Pescheria Nuova* (New fish market) was built in 1705 close to the *Scali del Pesce* where the fish was unloaded.

In the 1700s *Venezia Nuova* was the district of the Consuls of the Nations and of the most important international retailers who had the warehouses filled with goods from everywhere waiting to be shipped by sea to the most different destinations. The palaces along the canals had the turrets from which to see the ships approaching the port, moreover, they had the stores at the canal level to facilitate the unloading of the goods from the boats.

The *Venezia Nuova* district retains much of its original town planning and architectural features such as the bridges, narrow [lanes](./Lane "Lane"), the houses of the [nobility](./Nobility "Nobility"), churches as [Santa Caterina da Siena](./Santa_Caterina_da_Siena,_Livorno "Santa Caterina da Siena, Livorno") and [San Ferdinando](./San_Ferdinando,_Livorno "San Ferdinando, Livorno"), and a dense network of canals that once served to link its warehouses to the port. The [Livorno Courthouse](./Livorno_Courthouse "Livorno Courthouse") is located in Venezia Nuova.

#### *Monumento dei quattro mori*

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Livorno_Quattro_mori_monument_02.JPG/250px-Livorno_Quattro_mori_monument_02.JPG)](./File:Livorno_Quattro_mori_monument_02.JPG)

The *Monumento dei Quattro Mori* recently restored

The [Monument of the Four Moors](./Monument_of_the_Four_Moors "Monument of the Four Moors") is dedicated to [Ferdinando I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany](./Ferdinando_I_de'_Medici,_Grand_Duke_of_Tuscany "Ferdinando I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany"), and is one of the most popular monuments of Livorno. Ferdinando I commissioned it to Giovanni Bandini in 1595 to carry out a monument in white [Carrara marble](./Carrara_marble "Carrara marble") to represent him in the uniform of the [Grand master](./Grand_Master_(order) "Grand Master (order)") of the [Order of Saint Stephen](./Order_of_Saint_Stephen "Order of Saint Stephen") which in that period prevailed in several naval battles against the [Barbary pirates](./Barbary_pirates "Barbary pirates"). The monument was completed in 1599, shortly before the death of Bandini which occurred on 18 April,[[45]](./Livorno#cite_note-comunequattro-45)
and arrived to Livorno by sea from [Carrara](./Carrara "Carrara") in 1601.[[46]](./Livorno#cite_note-toscanago-46)

Ferdinando I projected to add four statues of moors prisoners at the pedestal of his monument and gave the task to [Pietro Tacca](./Pietro_Tacca "Pietro Tacca") in 1602[[45]](./Livorno#cite_note-comunequattro-45) but the monument remained in a corner of the square till 29 May 1617 when it was inaugurated by [Cosimo II de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany](./Cosimo_II_de'_Medici,_Grand_Duke_of_Tuscany "Cosimo II de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany").[[46]](./Livorno#cite_note-toscanago-46) In the meantime Tacca received the approval to add the four moors to the pedestal; the first two statues were fused in [Florence](./Florence "Florence") in 1622 and carried on the barges along the [Arno](./Arno "Arno") to Livorno; according to the tradition the young moor was named Morgiano and the older Alì Salentino;[[46]](./Livorno#cite_note-toscanago-46) the other two sculptures were installed in 1626. During the French occupation of Livorno, from 1796 to 1799, the monument was removed from Sextius Mollis commander of the French garrison because it represented an insult to the [tyranny](./Tyrant "Tyrant"), as soon as the French left the town the monument was put back in its former place.[[45]](./Livorno#cite_note-comunequattro-45)

During World War II the monument was transferred to a protected place in order to avoid being damaged by allied attacks, the statue of Ferdinando I was hidden in the [Pisa Charterhouse](./Pisa_Charterhouse "Pisa Charterhouse") and the four moors in the [Medici Villa at Poggio a Caiano](./Poggio_a_Caiano#The_Medici_villa "Poggio a Caiano").[[47]](./Livorno#cite_note-47)
The monument has been restored recently in 1990 and 2013.

#### *Acquedotto Leopoldino*

The *[Acquedotto Leopoldino](./Cisternoni_of_Livorno#Acquedotto_Leopoldino "Cisternoni of Livorno")* and the neoclassical cisterns of Livorno were part of a sophisticated scheme to provide water to Livorno.

#### *La Gran Conserva*

*[La Gran Conserva](./Cisternoni_of_Livorno#La_Gran_Conserva "Cisternoni of Livorno")*, or *Il Cisternone*, situated on what were the outskirts of 19th-century Livorno, is the largest and best known of the city's covered cisterns.

#### *Cisternino di città*

*[Cisternino di città](./Cisternoni_of_Livorno#Cisternino_di_città "Cisternoni of Livorno")* is an austere neoclassical design which was approved in 1837 and completed in 1848.

#### *Piazza della Repubblica*

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Piazza_della_Repubblica_dalla_Fortezza_Nuova_%28Livorno%29.JPG/250px-Piazza_della_Repubblica_dalla_Fortezza_Nuova_%28Livorno%29.JPG)](./File:Piazza_della_Repubblica_dalla_Fortezza_Nuova_(Livorno).JPG)

*Piazza della Repubblica*

At the beginning of the 19th century arose the need to connect the Medicean road system of the *[Pentagono del Buontalenti](./Livorno#Pentagono_del_Buontalenti)* to the new eastern districts of the town, on the other side of the *Fosso Reale*, and the requirement to dismantle the city gate *Porta a Pisa*. The solution adopted in 1844 was that of Luigi Bettarini which considered the coverage of the *Fosso Reale* with an imposing [vault](./Vault_(architecture) "Vault (architecture)"), 240 meters long and 90 meters wide,[[48]](./Livorno#cite_note-comunerepubblica-48) creating an elliptical paving. The portion of the canal covered by the new structure continued to be navigable.

The new square was commonly called *Piazza del [Voltone](./Vault_(architecture) "Vault (architecture)")* until 1850, then *Piazza dei [Granduchi](./List_of_rulers_of_Tuscany#Habsburg-Lorraine_Grand_Dukes_of_Tuscany,_1814–1860 "List of rulers of Tuscany")* in honour of the Lorraine dynasty until 1859, in the period of the [Italian unification](./Italian_unification "Italian unification") was named to *[Carlo Alberto](./Charles_Albert_of_Sardinia "Charles Albert of Sardinia")* until June 1946 when was given the current name *Piazza della [Repubblica](./Republic "Republic")*. The square, adorned with 52 marble benches, 92 pillars[[49]](./Livorno#cite_note-49) and two statues dedicated to [Ferdinand III](./Ferdinand_III,_Grand_Duke_of_Tuscany "Ferdinand III, Grand Duke of Tuscany") by Francesco Pozzi were inaugurated on 8 September 1847[[48]](./Livorno#cite_note-comunerepubblica-48) and that dedicated to [Leopold II](./Leopold_II,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Leopold II, Holy Roman Emperor") by Paolo Emilio Demi was installed on 6 June 1848.[[48]](./Livorno#cite_note-comunerepubblica-48) The statue of Leopoldo II was damaged by the crowd on 6 May 1849 and removed from the square because the Emperor was seen as the symbol of the Austrian domination; the statue was placed in *Piazza [XX Settembre](./Porta_Pia "Porta Pia")* in 1957.[[50]](./Livorno#cite_note-50)

#### *Terrazza Mascagni*

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Livorno_Terrazza_Mascagni_01_%40chesi.JPG/250px-Livorno_Terrazza_Mascagni_01_%40chesi.JPG)](./File:Livorno_Terrazza_Mascagni_01_@chesi.JPG)

*Terrazza Mascagni*

The *Terrazza Mascagni* is a wide sinuous belvedere toward the sea with views to the Livorno hills, the [Tuscan Archipelago](./Tuscan_Archipelago "Tuscan Archipelago") to [Corsica](./Corsica "Corsica"), and the [Port of Livorno](./Port_of_Livorno "Port of Livorno"). It is located on the site of the *Forte dei Cavalleggieri* (Cavalrymen Fort) built in the 17th century by [Cosimo I de' Medici](./Cosimo_I_de'_Medici,_Grand_Duke_of_Tuscany "Cosimo I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany") to deter pirate raids,[[51]](./Livorno#cite_note-51) subsequently replaced by a leisure park in the 1800s, and a heliotherapy centre in the early 1900s. A new [parterre](./Parterre "Parterre"), built between 1925 and 1928 by Enrico Salvais and Luigi Pastore, was formed by a series of flower beds and a walkway which follow the outline of the sea with numerous balustrades named after [Costanzo Ciano](./Costanzo_Ciano "Costanzo Ciano"). The *Terrazza* has a paved surface of 8,700 square meters formed by 34,800 black and white tiles placed as a [checkerboard](./Checkerboard "Checkerboard") and 4,100 [balusters](./Baluster "Baluster").[[52]](./Livorno#cite_note-52) In 1932, a [gazebo](./Gazebo "Gazebo") for musical performances was built in the large square;[[53]](./Livorno#cite_note-53) it was destroyed during World War II. In 1937 the [Livorno Aquarium](./Livorno#Acquario_comunale_"Diacinto_Cestoni") was constructed. After the war, the *Terrazza* was dedicated to [Pietro Mascagni](./Pietro_Mascagni "Pietro Mascagni") and in 1994 it underwent a complete restoration using the same kind of materials originally employed; the works were completed on 10 July 1998 with the reconstruction of the gazebo.[[54]](./Livorno#cite_note-54)

#### *Palazzo Comunale*

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c7/Livorno_Palazzo_Comunale_05_%40chesi.JPG/250px-Livorno_Palazzo_Comunale_05_%40chesi.JPG)](./File:Livorno_Palazzo_Comunale_05_@chesi.JPG)

*Palazzo Comunale* and the restored square

Livorno was elevated to the status of [city](./City "City") on 19 March 1606 by [Ferdinando I de' Medici](./Ferdinando_I_de'_Medici,_Grand_Duke_of_Tuscany "Ferdinando I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany"), the first [Gonfaloniere](./Gonfaloniere "Gonfaloniere") Bernardetto Borromei and the Community representatives held their meetings in the Church of Saint Mary and Saint Julia. On 13 June 1646 a building, placed in *Via del Porticciolo*, was purchased for the sum of seven thousand [ducats](./Ducat "Ducat"), in order to accommodate the Community. It was evident that it was inadequate to the task and the Council deliberated, on 27 January 1720, the construction of the new town hall on the project by Giovanni del Fantasia.[[55]](./Livorno#cite_note-55)

The new neo-renaissance palace, positioned between *Palazzo della Dogana* and *Palazzo Granducale* on the north side of *Piazza d’Arme*, was partially destroyed by the 1742 earthquake. Restored in 1745 by Bernardino Ciurini and Antonio Fabbri a double white marble stairway and a small bell tower on the top of the façade were added. In 1867 the complex was enlarged with the acquisition of three other buildings in the back. With the settlement of the [Podestà](./Podestà "Podestà") in the [fascist](./Fascist "Fascist") period was carried out a new enlargement in 1929 by Enrico Salvais and Luigi Pastore transforming the adjacent former fire station in the council hall. Damaged by the bombing during World War II it was rebuilt and renovated under the direction of Primavera and was inaugurated in 1949 by the mayor Furio Diaz.[[56]](./Livorno#cite_note-56)

### Religious architecture

#### Cathedral of Saint Francis of Assisi

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Livorno_Piazza_Grande_02_%40chesi.JPG/250px-Livorno_Piazza_Grande_02_%40chesi.JPG)](./File:Livorno_Piazza_Grande_02_@chesi.JPG)

The Cathedral of Saint Francis of Assisi and *Piazza Grande* restored

The cathedral of the town, commonly called [Duomo di Livorno](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duomo%20di%20Livorno "it:Duomo di Livorno"), is dedicated to [Francis of Assisi](./Francis_of_Assisi "Francis of Assisi"), [Mary, mother of Jesus](./Mary_(mother_of_Jesus) "Mary (mother of Jesus)"), and [Julia of Corsica](./Julia_of_Corsica "Julia of Corsica"), and was built in a central position of the [Pentagono del Buontalenti](./Livorno#Pentagono_del_Buontalenti) on the south side of Piazza Grande once named Piazza d’Arme. The original plan was drawn up by [Bernardo Buontalenti](./Bernardo_Buontalenti "Bernardo Buontalenti") when he projected the new town. The construction began in June 1581 on a reviewed plan by [Alessandro Pieroni](./Alessandro_Pieroni "Alessandro Pieroni") under the direction of Antonio Cantagallina. The church had a rectangular plant with a single nave, the original wooden ceiling, executed from 1610 to 1614, was carved by Vincenzo Ricordati[[57]](./Livorno#cite_note-57) and gilded with seven inserted paintings. [Jacopo Ligozzi](./Jacopo_Ligozzi "Jacopo Ligozzi"), [Domenico Cresti](./Domenico_Cresti "Domenico Cresti") and [Jacopo Chimenti](./Jacopo_Chimenti "Jacopo Chimenti") decorated, from 1610 to 1614, three large paintings representing "St Francis with Child and the Virgin", the "Assumption of Mary" and the "Apotheosis of Ste Julia", the other four paintings were works by minor artists.[[58]](./Livorno#cite_note-livornoyoungdom-58) The simply façade had a marble porch with twin Doric columns surmounted by a terrace added in 1605 on a project by Alessandro Pieroni.[[59]](./Livorno#cite_note-59)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Duomo_Livorno%2C_interno.JPG/250px-Duomo_Livorno%2C_interno.JPG)](./File:Duomo_Livorno,_interno.JPG)

Cathedral's nave

The church was consecrated on 19 February 1606 by [Monsignor](./Monsignor "Monsignor") Nunzio Antonio Grimani; on request by [Ferdinando II de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany](./Ferdinando_II_de'_Medici,_Grand_Duke_of_Tuscany "Ferdinando II de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany"), in 1629, was elevated to [collegiate church](./Collegiate_church "Collegiate church") and the *Curato* was substituted from a *Proposto* having the functions of the Vicar of the [archbishop of Pisa](./Roman_Catholic_Archdiocese_of_Pisa "Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Pisa").[[58]](./Livorno#cite_note-livornoyoungdom-58)
The plant of the church was modified in [Christian cross](./Christian_cross "Christian cross") when in 1716 was added the first of two lateral chapels. The left side chapel, dedicated to the [Eucharist](./Eucharist "Eucharist"), was built on a project by [Giovanni del Fantasia](./Giovanni_del_Fantasia "Giovanni del Fantasia") with frescoes by Giovanni Maria Terreni and the altar attributed to [Giovanni Baratta](./Giovanni_Baratta "Giovanni Baratta"), The right side chapel, dedicated to [Immaculate Conception](./Immaculate_Conception "Immaculate Conception"), was built in 1727 and was decorated with paintings by [Luigi Ademollo](./Luigi_Ademollo "Luigi Ademollo"). The Collegiata in 1806 was elevated to [cathedral](./Cathedral "Cathedral") and in 1817 was added the bell tower 50 meters high on project by Gaspero Pampaloni.[[60]](./Livorno#cite_note-60)
The cathedral was completely destroyed in 1943 from the Allied bombardment during World War II; it was then rebuilt respecting the original structure except for the two marble porches added to the [transepts](./Transept "Transept") and was consecrated on 21 December 1952 by [Bishop Giovanni Piccioni](./Roman_Catholic_Diocese_of_Livorno#Ordinaries "Roman Catholic Diocese of Livorno").[[58]](./Livorno#cite_note-livornoyoungdom-58)

Since 2006, on the occasion of the bicentennial of the [Roman Catholic Diocese of Livorno](./Roman_Catholic_Diocese_of_Livorno "Roman Catholic Diocese of Livorno"), the "Christ Crowned with Thorns", by [Fra Angelico](./Fra_Angelico "Fra Angelico"), was displayed in the Chapel of the Eucharist.

#### Church of the Madonna

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Livorno_Chiesa_della_Madonna_01_%40chesi.JPG/250px-Livorno_Chiesa_della_Madonna_01_%40chesi.JPG)](./File:Livorno_Chiesa_della_Madonna_01_@chesi.JPG)

Church of the Madonna

The Church of the Madonna is placed on the street of the same name which connects directly the city centre with the district *[Venezia Nuova](./Livorno#Venezia_Nuova)* through the [John of Nepomuk](./John_of_Nepomuk "John of Nepomuk") bridge. According to tradition the church was built to host the statute of [Our Lady of Mount Carmel](./Our_Lady_of_Mount_Carmel "Our Lady of Mount Carmel") subtracted from a Turkish ship.[[61]](./Livorno#cite_note-61) The church was important as it was a place of worship for foreign communities. [Ferdinando I de' Medici](./Ferdinando_I_de'_Medici,_Grand_Duke_of_Tuscany "Ferdinando I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany") gave the church to the [Franciscan](./Franciscan "Franciscan") which had the nearby Oratory of Saints Cosmas and Damian. The construction began on 25 March 1607 on a project by [Alessandro Pieroni](./Alessandro_Pieroni "Alessandro Pieroni") and was completed in 1611; the church at first was dedicated to [Saint Mary](./Mary_(mother_of_Jesus) "Mary (mother of Jesus)"), [Saint Francis](./Francis_of_Assisi "Francis of Assisi") and [Saints Cosmas and Damian](./Saints_Cosmas_and_Damian "Saints Cosmas and Damian") but in 1638 was dedicated to the [Immaculate Conception](./Immaculate_Conception "Immaculate Conception") following enlargement of the building.

The church has a rectangular plan with a single nave and [groin vault](./Groin_vault "Groin vault"), on each side, there are the three altars of the foreign Nations. The altar of the French Nation was built in 1613 and the painting, by Matteo Rosselli, represents [Saint Louis](./Louis_IX_of_France "Louis IX of France"). The altar of the Corsican Nation, which at the time was under the control of the [Republic of Genoa](./Republic_of_Genoa "Republic of Genoa"), has a painting representing [John the Evangelist](./John_the_Evangelist "John the Evangelist"). The altar of the Portuguese Nation, built in the 17th century, had a wooden statue of Saint Mary until 1728 when this was positioned near the main altar and replaced by one of [Anthony of Padua](./Anthony_of_Padua "Anthony of Padua"). The altar of the Dutch-German Nation is dedicated to [Andrew the Apostle](./Andrew_the_Apostle "Andrew the Apostle").[[62]](./Livorno#cite_note-62) Outside the body of the building, separated by a railing, is a Chapel dedicate to the *[Madonna di Montenero](./Sanctuary_of_Montenero "Sanctuary of Montenero")* built in 1631.[[63]](./Livorno#cite_note-63) The simple façade was covered in white marble in 1972.

#### Church of the Most Holy Annunciation

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Livorno_Chiesa_Santissima_Annunziata_04_%40chesi.JPG/250px-Livorno_Chiesa_Santissima_Annunziata_04_%40chesi.JPG)](./File:Livorno_Chiesa_Santissima_Annunziata_04_@chesi.JPG)

*Chiesa della Santissima Annunziata*

The Church of the [Most Holy Annunciation](./Annunciation "Annunciation") is located in the central street of *Via della Madonna*, not far from the [Armenian community](./Livorno#Armenian_community) Church of [Gregory the Illuminator](./Gregory_the_Illuminator "Gregory the Illuminator") and the [Church of the Madonna](./Livorno#Church_of_the_Madonna). The church is called Unite Greeks too because was the worship place for the [Greek community](./Livorno#Greek_community) of [Byzantine Rite](./Byzantine_Rite "Byzantine Rite") who once lived in Livorno. At the end of the 16th century, numerous Greeks came to Tuscany to take service aboard the [galleys](./Galley "Galley") of the [Order of Saint Stephen](./Order_of_Saint_Stephen "Order of Saint Stephen"). The church was built in 1601 on a project by [Alessandro Pieroni](./Alessandro_Pieroni "Alessandro Pieroni"), was completed in 1605 and consecrated on 25 March 1606.[[64]](./Livorno#cite_note-64) The [baroque](./Baroque "Baroque") façade was built in 1708 presumably on a project by [Giovanni Baratta](./Giovanni_Baratta "Giovanni Baratta") with a triangular [pediment](./Pediment "Pediment") and [Doric order](./Doric_order "Doric order") and was decorated by the statues of Meekness and Innocence by Andrea Vaccà. The interior has a single nave and the ceiling is adorned by a [coffer](./Coffer "Coffer") structure with a central painting representing the Annunciation by Giovanni Domenico Ferretti (1750).[[65]](./Livorno#cite_note-65) The precious wooden [Iconostasis](./Iconostasis "Iconostasis") in Byzantine style date back to 1641 and has three doors painted by Agostino Wanonbrachen in 1751; on the central door is represented the Most Holy Annunciation and [Basil of Caesarea](./Basil_of_Caesarea "Basil of Caesarea"), [Gregory of Nazianzus](./Gregory_of_Nazianzus "Gregory of Nazianzus"), [John Chrysostom](./John_Chrysostom "John Chrysostom") and [Athanasius of Alexandria](./Athanasius_of_Alexandria "Athanasius of Alexandria"); in the right door is painted the [Nativity of Jesus](./Nativity_of_Jesus "Nativity of Jesus") and the four Apostles, in the left door is represented the [Adoration of the Shepherds](./Adoration_of_the_Shepherds "Adoration of the Shepherds").[[66]](./Livorno#cite_note-66)
The church was entirely destroyed by the bombings during World War II and the restoration was completed in 1985.

#### Other Religious Structures

* [Santa Caterina da Siena](./Santa_Caterina_da_Siena,_Livorno "Santa Caterina da Siena, Livorno"): Baroque church in the centre of Livorno, in *Venezia Nuova* district.
* [San Ferdinando](./San_Ferdinando,_Livorno "San Ferdinando, Livorno"): Baroque church located also in *Venezia Nuova* district next to the Piazza del Luogo Pio.
* [San Giovanni Battista](./San_Giovanni_Battista,_Livorno "San Giovanni Battista, Livorno"): [Baroque](./Baroque_architecture "Baroque architecture")-[Mannerist](./Mannerism "Mannerism") church located at the crossing of *Via San Giovanni* and *Via Carraia* in central Livorno.
* [Santa Maria del Soccorso](./Santa_Maria_del_Soccorso,_Livorno "Santa Maria del Soccorso, Livorno"): [Neoclassical](./Neoclassicism "Neoclassicism") Marian votive church in central Livorno. The tall brick church façade is located scenically at the end of *Via Magenta*, and has a park surrounding it. In front is a Monument to Fallen Soldiers (*caduti*) in the first World War.
* [Old English Cemetery](./Old_English_Cemetery,_Livorno "Old English Cemetery, Livorno"): oldest foreign Protestant burial ground in Italy. It was founded around 1645 and contains over 300 Carrara marble graves of notable people from 10 different nationalities. [Tobias Smollett](./Tobias_Smollett "Tobias Smollett") and [Francis Horner](./Francis_Horner "Francis Horner") were buried here, but also some of the friends of [Byron](./George_Gordon_Byron "George Gordon Byron") and [Shelley](./Percy_Bysshe_Shelley "Percy Bysshe Shelley") and the husband of [Saint Elizabeth Seton](./Elizabeth_Ann_Seton "Elizabeth Ann Seton"). The cemetery was closed in 1839 and a new one, still active, was opened.
* [Sanctuary of Montenero](./Sanctuary_of_Montenero "Sanctuary of Montenero"): Marian sanctuary atop a hill outside Livorno, dedicated to [Our Lady of Graces](./Our_Lady_of_Graces "Our Lady of Graces"), the patron saint of Tuscany, is a destination for [pilgrims](./Pilgrims "Pilgrims"). It is famous for the adjacent gallery, decorated with [ex-voto](./Ex-voto "Ex-voto"), chiefly related to events of miraculous rescues of people at sea.
* [Temple of the Dutch German Congregation](./Temple_of_the_Dutch_German_Congregation "Temple of the Dutch German Congregation"): known more simply as the Dutch-German Church, is situated in Livorno, on the stretch of the *Fosso Reale* canal that runs between *Piazza della Repubblica* and *Piazza Cavour*.
* [Synagogue of Livorno](./Synagogue_of_Livorno "Synagogue of Livorno"): main [Jewish](./Judaism "Judaism") place of worship in Livorno, located in *Piazza [Elijah Benamozegh](./Elijah_Benamozegh "Elijah Benamozegh")*.

### Military architecture

#### *Fortezza Vecchia*

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Livorno_-_Fortezza_Vecchia.jpg/250px-Livorno_-_Fortezza_Vecchia.jpg)](./File:Livorno_-_Fortezza_Vecchia.jpg)

*Fortezza Vecchia*

The origin of *[Fortezza Vecchia](./Old_Fortress,_Livorno "Old Fortress, Livorno")* takes place not far from what once was *Porto Pisano* (Pisan Port) where a square tower was built in 1077, on request of [Matilda of Tuscany](./Matilda_of_Tuscany "Matilda of Tuscany"), on the remains of a Roman tower; in 1241 the Pisans built a massive cylindrical tower, 30 meters high erroneously called *[Mastio](./Keep "Keep") di Matilde* (Matilda keep).
[[67]](./Livorno#cite_note-Livornina-67) Pisa realized the strategic importance of the castle of Livorno which owned since 1103 and in 1377 the [Doge](./Doge_(title) "Doge (title)") *Gambacorti* of the [Republic of Pisa](./Republic_of_Pisa "Republic of Pisa") built a quadrangular Fort called *Quadratura dei Pisani* (Quartered of the Pisans) on plans attributed to *Puccio di Landuccio* and *Francesco di Giovanni Giordani*. In 1392 this fort was connected to a wall in order to defend better the town and the *[Darsena](./Dock_(maritime) "Dock (maritime)")*.[[68]](./Livorno#cite_note-68) Livorno, in 1405, was sold to Genoa which reinforced the defences, building three forts under the Quartered, afterwards Livorno was bought from [Florence](./Florence "Florence") on 28 August 1421 at the price of 100.000 [Tuscan florin](./Tuscan_florin "Tuscan florin").[[10]](./Livorno#cite_note-treccanilivorno-10)
The project to build *Fortezza Vecchia* was commissioned to [Antonio da Sangallo the Elder](./Antonio_da_Sangallo_the_Elder "Antonio da Sangallo the Elder") in 1506, the fortress had to incorporate the existing Pisan and Genovese constructions.[[69]](./Livorno#cite_note-69)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Livorno_Fortezza_Vecchia_bastione_della_Canaviglia_02_%40chesi.JPG/250px-Livorno_Fortezza_Vecchia_bastione_della_Canaviglia_02_%40chesi.JPG)](./File:Livorno_Fortezza_Vecchia_bastione_della_Canaviglia_02_@chesi.JPG)

Matilda keep and *Canaviglia* bastion

The works started in 1518 on the order of [Cardinal Giulio De' Medici](./Pope_Clement_VII "Pope Clement VII") under the supervision of *Nicolao da Pietrasanta*. The construction was suspended since the popular revolt forced the [Medici in exile](./House_of_Medici#16th_century "House of Medici") and was resumed in 1530 on their return. *Fortezza Vecchia* is a massive fortification completed on 1 April 1534 under *[Alessandro de' Medici](./Alessandro_de'_Medici,_Duke_of_Florence "Alessandro de' Medici, Duke of Florence")*; it was built in red-brick with sloping walls and the interposition of clear stones, it has a quadrangular plant with a perimeter of 1500 meters and was equipped with 24 cannons to protect each side.[[67]](./Livorno#cite_note-Livornina-67) One of the corners directs inside to join the Quartered of the Pisans and Matilda and Genoa keep; the three others are protected by triangular [bastions](./Bastion "Bastion") with rounded tips. The bastion towards the north is called *Capitana* because there moored the main [Galley](./Galley "Galley"), to the east is *Ampolletta* since housed the sand-glass used to control the guard duty, to the west is the *Canaviglia* derived from *Cavaniglia* the name of the commander of the galleys of the Grand Ducky of Tuscany. The land on the side toward the town was excavated in order to have the fortress surrounded by the sea for better defence. *[Cosimo I de' Medici](./Cosimo_I_de'_Medici,_Grand_Duke_of_Tuscany "Cosimo I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany")* built in 1544 an imposing palace, overlooking the *[Vecchia Darsena](./Port_of_Livorno#Vecchia_Darsena "Port of Livorno")*, above the Quartered of the Pisans which went destroyed during World War II. The successor [Francesco I de' Medici](./Francesco_I_de'_Medici,_Grand_Duke_of_Tuscany "Francesco I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany") built a small palace toward the sea, later became *[Porto Mediceo](./Port_of_Livorno#Porto_Mediceo "Port of Livorno")*, on the top of Canaviglia bastion situated at the entrance of *Vecchia Darsena*. On the opposite side was built a church dedicated to Saint Francis where on 19 March 1606 *[Ferdinando I de' Medici](./Ferdinando_I_de'_Medici,_Grand_Duke_of_Tuscany "Ferdinando I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany")* elevated Livorno to the status of [city](./City "City").[[67]](./Livorno#cite_note-Livornina-67) *Fortezza Vecchia* changed its function to the coming of the [House of Habsburg-Lorraine](./Grand_Duchy_of_Tuscany#House_of_Habsburg-Lorraine "Grand Duchy of Tuscany") in 1737, by a defensive structure to a military college for officers of the Army of the [Grand Duchy of Tuscany](./Grand_Duchy_of_Tuscany "Grand Duchy of Tuscany") (1769) and afterwards in garrison (1795).

#### *Fortezza Nuova*

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Livorno-Fortezza_Nuova.jpg/250px-Livorno-Fortezza_Nuova.jpg)](./File:Livorno-Fortezza_Nuova.jpg)

*Fortezza Nuova*

The origin of *Fortezza Nuova* (New fortress) took place towards the end of the 1500s, by the adjustment of the *Baluardo [San Francesco](./Francis_of_Assisi "Francis of Assisi")* (Saint Francis rampart) and the *Baluardo [Santa Barbara](./Saint_Barbara "Saint Barbara")* (Saint Barbara rampant). The project was commissioned by [Cosimo I](./Cosimo_I_de'_Medici,_Grand_Duke_of_Tuscany "Cosimo I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany") to [Bernardo Buontalenti](./Bernardo_Buontalenti "Bernardo Buontalenti") with the intention to develop a new urban plan of the town that led to a pentagonal shape surrounded by canals.

The original project was then modified by [Don Giovanni de' Medici](./Don_Giovanni_de'_Medici "Don Giovanni de' Medici"), Claudio Cogorano and [Alessandro Pieroni](./Alessandro_Pieroni "Alessandro Pieroni") to allow the construction of the *Fortezza Nuova* in order to strengthen the military apparatus of the town. The works started on 10 January 1590 and ended in 1604, the result is a considerable fortification, in stones and red bricks, with a polygonal plant surrounded by water; the new modification brought to the construction of the *Forte San Pietro* (Saint Peter fort) to defend the *Venezia Nuova* quarter.
[[70]](./Livorno#cite_note-70)

In 1629 part of the fortress was demolished to permit the building of the *Venezia Nuova* and the *San Marco* quarters that was commissioned by [Ferdinando II](./Ferdinando_II_de'_Medici,_Grand_Duke_of_Tuscany "Ferdinando II de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany").
[[71]](./Livorno#cite_note-71)
The *Fortezza Nuova* has been used for military purpose until the end of World War II, inside were built barracks and warehouses and a chapel dedicated to the [Immaculate Conception](./Immaculate_Conception "Immaculate Conception").[[72]](./Livorno#cite_note-72)

The fortress was heavily damaged during World War II with the destruction of most parts of the buildings, the restoration was completed in 1972 and the superior part is used at present as a public park and centre for events and displays.

#### *Pentagono del Buontalenti*

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/02/Citt%C3%A0_pentagonale_-Copia_del_progetto_di_B.Buontalenti-.png/330px-Citt%C3%A0_pentagonale_-Copia_del_progetto_di_B.Buontalenti-.png)](./File:Città_pentagonale_-Copia_del_progetto_di_B.Buontalenti-.png)

The copy of the project by Buontalenti

[Francesco I de' Medici](./Francesco_I_de'_Medici,_Grand_Duke_of_Tuscany "Francesco I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany") gave to [Bernardo Buontalenti](./Bernardo_Buontalenti "Bernardo Buontalenti") in 1575 the task to project the [ideal town](./Ideal_town "Ideal town") in order to transform Livorno from a fishing village in a fortified town to accommodate 12,000 inhabitants,[[73]](./Livorno#cite_note-73) to include the original settlement and the *Fortezza Vecchia*, capable to become the trade centre of the [Grand Duchy of Tuscany](./Grand_Duchy_of_Tuscany "Grand Duchy of Tuscany"). The development of the project led to a pentagonal plant as in use in the [Renaissance](./Renaissance "Renaissance") period, each side 600 meters long, with defensive walls, rampant and five bastions at the vertices, surrounded by canals; the fifth bastion coincided with *[Fortezza Vecchia](./Livorno#Fortezza_Vecchia)*. The plan gave no information regarding the function of the new urban area, indicating only a series of building blocks within a road system absolutely orthogonal, [cardo](./Cardo "Cardo") and [Decumanus Maximus](./Decumanus_Maximus "Decumanus Maximus").[[74]](./Livorno#cite_note-74)
The road axis from north to south (cardo) underline the direction that united the centre of the town with a significant place as the [Sanctuary of Montenero](./Sanctuary_of_Montenero "Sanctuary of Montenero"); the axis from west to east (decumanus) linked the *Baluardo Santa Giulia* to *Baluardo Sant’Andrea*.[[75]](./Livorno#cite_note-architetto_livorno-75)
In August 1576 was created the Office of the *Fabbrica di Livorno* with the task of supervising the construction and Alessandro Puccini was the chief superintendent.[[76]](./Livorno#cite_note-76)

Francesco I de' Medici laid the first stone for the construction of the *Baluardo di San Francesco* (Saint Francis rampant) of the new town on 28 March 1577; the works went on with several changes compared with the original plan including the construction of the *[Fortezza Nuova](./Livorno#Fortezza_Nuova)*.[[75]](./Livorno#cite_note-architetto_livorno-75)
Livorno became a town, encircled by the navigable *[Fosso](./Canal "Canal") Reale* (Royal canal), with numerous palaces, warehouse, garrisons and custom-houses. The central street at that time was *Via Ferdinanda* extended for 750 meters, later called *Via Grande*, from *[Porta](./City_gate "City gate") Colonnella* (Colonella city gate), in the proximity of *[Vecchia Darsena](./Port_of_Livorno#Vecchia_Darsena "Port of Livorno")*, to *Porta Pisana* (Pisan city gate). The *Baluardo Sant’Andrea* was initiated in 1578 while the *Baluardo Santa Giulia* started in 1582.[[77]](./Livorno#cite_note-77)

In 1594 it was decided to create a huge square, at halfway of *Via Ferdinanda*, where to build the church of the new town. The church, which was built in a central position on the south side of *Piazza d’Arme*, later *Piazza Grande*, was completed in 1602 under the direction of Antonio Cantagaliina and [Alessandro Pieroni](./Alessandro_Pieroni "Alessandro Pieroni"). *Piazza d’Arme* was completed and enlarged with the old *Porticciolo dei Genovesi* (Port of Genovesi) filled up with earth to make room to the building called *Tre Palazzi* (Three palaces); the square was adorned with a series of marble arcades attributed to Alessandro Pieroni.
[[78]](./Livorno#cite_note-78) The *Palazzo del [Picchetto](./Picket_(military) "Picket (military)")* was built, on plan by [Giovanni Battista Foggini](./Giovanni_Battista_Foggini "Giovanni Battista Foggini") and Giovanni del Fantasia in 1707, at the end of *Via Ferdinanda* in the proximity of *Porta Pisana*.

Infrastructure
--------------

### Airport

The nearest airport is the main airport of Tuscany, [Pisa International Airport](./Pisa_International_Airport "Pisa International Airport"), which is about 20 kilometres (12 mi) away.

### Buses

Since 1875 Livorno has ever had a public transport system managed by some companies such as [ATAM](./Azienda_Trasporti_Autofiloviari_Municipale "Azienda Trasporti Autofiloviari Municipale"), [ACIT](./Azienda_Consorziale_Interprovinciale_Trasporti "Azienda Consorziale Interprovinciale Trasporti"), [ATL](./Azienda_Trasporti_Livornese "Azienda Trasporti Livornese") and [CTT Nord](./CTT_Nord "CTT Nord") that changed over the years.
Livorno bus network, as the entire [Regione Toscana](./Regione_Toscana "Regione Toscana"), is performed by [Autolinee Toscane](./Autolinee_Toscane "Autolinee Toscane") which manages, since 1 November 2021,[[79]](./Livorno#cite_note-79) two High Mobility Lines (*LAM Blu* and *LAM Rossa*), seventeen urban lines, one school line and six suburban routes departing from Livorno across the [Province](./Province_of_Livorno "Province of Livorno"). Autolinee Toscane operates a [funicular](./Montenero_funicular "Montenero funicular") which connect lower Montenero to the [Sanctuary](./Sanctuary_of_Montenero "Sanctuary of Montenero").[[80]](./Livorno#cite_note-80)[[81]](./Livorno#cite_note-81)

### Port

The [Port of Livorno](./Port_of_Livorno "Port of Livorno") is one of the largest seaports both in Italy and the Mediterranean Sea as a whole.
The Port has regular ferry links of the following operators with the following cities:

* [Corsica Ferries - Sardinia Ferries](./Corsica_Ferries_-_Sardinia_Ferries "Corsica Ferries - Sardinia Ferries") to [Golfo Aranci](./Golfo_Aranci "Golfo Aranci") and [Bastia](./Bastia "Bastia")
* [Grimaldi Lines](./Grimaldi_Group "Grimaldi Group") to [Barcelona](./Barcelona "Barcelona") and [Tangier](./Tangier "Tangier")
* [Moby Lines](./Moby_Lines "Moby Lines") to [Olbia](./Olbia "Olbia") and [Bastia](./Bastia "Bastia")
* [Toremar](./Toremar "Toremar") to [Capraia](./Capraia "Capraia")

### Trains

The city is served by [Livorno Centrale station](./Livorno_Centrale_railway_station "Livorno Centrale railway station").

Education
---------

### Schools

#### *Istituto Tecnico Industriale "Galileo Galilei"*

The [Industrial Technical Institute](./Secondary_education_in_Italy#Istituto_tecnico "Secondary education in Italy") named to [Galileo Galilei](./Galileo_Galilei "Galileo Galilei") was founded in 1825 as a School of Arts and Crafts in order to prepare the youngs to a profession in the sector of the mechanic industry as in the decorative arts. In 1923 the [Gentile Reform](./Gentile_Reform "Gentile Reform") transformed the school in an Industrial Technical Institute for [mechanics](./Mechanics "Mechanics") and [electrical engineering](./Electrical_engineering "Electrical engineering"), and in 1947 was added [chemistry](./Chemistry "Chemistry"). In the following years other specialities were added as [physics](./Physics "Physics"), [electronics](./Electronics "Electronics"), [biology](./Biology "Biology"), [nuclear physics](./Nuclear_physics "Nuclear physics") and [informatics](./Informatics "Informatics"). The institute is structured with 32 laboratories, 8 special school-rooms, library, film library, gymnasiums and machine-shops.[[82]](./Livorno#cite_note-82)

#### *Istituto Nautico "Alfredo Cappellini"*

The Nautical Institute Alfredo Cappellini was formed on 13 December 1863, with a Royal Law and it was the first Technical Institute in the [Province of Livorno](./Province_of_Livorno "Province of Livorno"). In 1921 it was transferred under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Navy then returned to the Ministry of Education. The school give the professional preparation to form the [Merchant navy](./Merchant_navy "Merchant navy") Officers.

#### *Liceo Classico "Niccolini Palli"*

The *[Liceo Classico](./Liceo_Classico "Liceo Classico") [Niccolini](./Giovanni_Battista_Niccolini "Giovanni Battista Niccolini")* was established on 10 March 1860 by law of [Terenzio Mamiani](./Terenzio,_Count_Mamiani_della_Rovere "Terenzio, Count Mamiani della Rovere"), then Ministry of the Public Instruction. The first *[Preside](./Dean_(education) "Dean (education)")* elected was Luigi De Steffani who remained in charge from 1862 to 1867. The Liceo was entitled to [Giovanni Battista Niccolini](./Giovanni_Battista_Niccolini "Giovanni Battista Niccolini"), [Ugo Foscolo](./Ugo_Foscolo "Ugo Foscolo")'s friend, in 1862; in 1883 it was named to [Francesco Domenico Guerrazzi](./Francesco_Domenico_Guerrazzi "Francesco Domenico Guerrazzi"); the name came into effect in 1889 and remained until the unification of the *Liceo* with the *[Istituto magistrale](./Liceo_delle_scienze_umane "Liceo delle scienze umane")*. The most famous professor was [Giovanni Pascoli](./Giovanni_Pascoli "Giovanni Pascoli") who taught [Greek](./Greek_language "Greek language") and [Latin](./Latin "Latin") from 1887 to 1895. Among the pupils were [Pietro Mascagni](./Pietro_Mascagni "Pietro Mascagni"), [Guglielmo Marconi](./Guglielmo_Marconi "Guglielmo Marconi"), [Amedeo Modigliani](./Amedeo_Modigliani "Amedeo Modigliani"), [Giosuè Borsi](./Giosuè_Borsi?action=edit&redlink=1 "Giosuè Borsi") and [Carlo Azeglio Ciampi](./Carlo_Azeglio_Ciampi "Carlo Azeglio Ciampi"), who was teacher in 1945.[[83]](./Livorno#cite_note-83)

### Library

Further information on the library: [Villa Fabbricotti](./Villa_Fabbricotti "Villa Fabbricotti")

#### Biblioteca Labronica

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Livorno_Villa_Fabbricotti_01.JPG/250px-Livorno_Villa_Fabbricotti_01.JPG)](./File:Livorno_Villa_Fabbricotti_01.JPG)

*Biblioteca Labronica F.D. Guerrazzi*

The [Biblioteca Labronica](./Biblioteca_Labronica "Biblioteca Labronica") [[it](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblioteca%20Labronica "it:Biblioteca Labronica")] on the Viale della Libertà was founded in 1816, by the fellows of the *Accademia Labronica*, which was made public in 1840 and it was given to the Comune in 1854.[[84]](./Livorno#cite_note-84)[[85]](./Livorno#cite_note-iccu-85) The civic library was dedicated to Francesco Domenico Guerrazzi in 1923[[86]](./Livorno#cite_note-86) and take place in *Villa Fabbricotti*. According to the tradition, the origin of the villa date back to the Medicean period when an edifice was built as a suburban residence for [Ferdinando II de' Medici](./Ferdinando_II_de'_Medici "Ferdinando II de' Medici"). *Villa Fabbricotti* received the name from its last owner Bernardo Fabbricotti from [Carrara](./Carrara "Carrara"), who acquired it from the English merchant Thomas Lloyd in 1881. Fabbricotti, following to adverse economic affairs, sold the Villa and the park to the [Comune](./Comune "Comune") in 1936. During World War II the building was used by the German command as headquarters, and later taken by the American forces;[[87]](./Livorno#cite_note-87) in the post-war period was restored in order to adapt it into library. In the warehouse of the *Biblioteca Labronica* are stored: 120,000 books, 1,500 [manuscripts](./Manuscript "Manuscript"), 117 [incunables](./Incunable "Incunable"), 2,000 cinquecentine (is a book printed in the 16th century) and 60,000 [autographs](./Autograph "Autograph"); the library is organized with reading rooms with 80 places of capacity, 18 seats for consultation of manuscripts, 4 internet positions and a conference room with 60 seats. The library has a collection of autographs including those of [Galileo Galilei](./Galileo_Galilei "Galileo Galilei") and [Giacomo Leopardi](./Giacomo_Leopardi "Giacomo Leopardi"), manuscripts by [Ugo Foscolo](./Ugo_Foscolo "Ugo Foscolo"), and ancient books printed in Livorno since the 17th century, including the *[Encyclopédie](./Encyclopédie "Encyclopédie")* printed in 1770 in Livorno by the ancient *Bagno dei forzati* ([Gaol](./Gaol "Gaol") of the [convicts](./Convicts "Convicts")).[[88]](./Livorno#cite_note-88)

**Livorno** (Italian: [[liˈvorno]](./Help:IPA/Italian "Help:IPA/Italian") [ⓘ](/wiki/File:It-Livorno.ogg "File:It-Livorno.ogg")) is a port city on the [Ligurian Sea](./Ligurian_Sea "Ligurian Sea")[[2]](./Livorno#cite_note-2) on the western coast of the [Tuscany](./Tuscany "Tuscany") region of [Italy](./Italy "Italy").[[3]](./Livorno#cite_note-3) It is the capital of the [Province of Livorno](./Province_of_Livorno "Province of Livorno"), having a population of 152,916 residents as of 2025.[[1]](./Livorno#cite_note-population-1) It is traditionally known in English as **Leghorn** (pronounced [/lɛˈɡɔːrn/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [*leg-ORN*](./Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"),[[4]](./Livorno#cite_note-Cham20-4)[[5]](./Livorno#cite_note-collins-concise-5) [/ˈlɛɡhɔːrn/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [*LEG-horn*](./Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")[[6]](./Livorno#cite_note-oxf-6) or [/ˈlɛɡərn/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [*LEG-ərn*](./Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")).[[7]](./Livorno#cite_note-7)[[8]](./Livorno#cite_note-8)

During the [Renaissance](./Italian_Renaissance "Italian Renaissance"), Livorno was designed as an "[ideal town](./Ideal_town "Ideal town")". Developing considerably from the second half of the [16th century](./16th_century "16th century") by the will of the [House of Medici](./House_of_Medici "House of Medici"), Livorno was an important [free port](./Free_port "Free port"). Its intense commercial activity was largely dominated by foreign traders. Also the seat of consulates and shipping companies, it became the main port-city of the [Grand Duchy of Tuscany](./Grand_Duchy_of_Tuscany "Grand Duchy of Tuscany").[[9]](./Livorno#cite_note-9) The high status of a multiethnic and multicultural Livorno lasted until the second half of the nineteenth century, when it was surpassed by other cities. Evidence of that prosperous time can be seen in the many churches, villas, and palaces of the city.[[10]](./Livorno#cite_note-treccanilivorno-10)

Livorno is considered to be the most modern among all the Tuscan cities, and is the third most-populous of the region, after [Florence](./Florence "Florence") and [Prato](./Prato "Prato").[[11]](./Livorno#cite_note-11)[[12]](./Livorno#cite_note-12)

History
-------
