Infrastructure
--------------

### Airport

The nearest airport is the main airport of Tuscany, [Pisa International Airport](./Pisa_International_Airport "Pisa International Airport"), which is about 20 kilometres (12 mi) away.

### Buses

Since 1875 Livorno has ever had a public transport system managed by some companies such as [ATAM](./Azienda_Trasporti_Autofiloviari_Municipale "Azienda Trasporti Autofiloviari Municipale"), [ACIT](./Azienda_Consorziale_Interprovinciale_Trasporti "Azienda Consorziale Interprovinciale Trasporti"), [ATL](./Azienda_Trasporti_Livornese "Azienda Trasporti Livornese") and [CTT Nord](./CTT_Nord "CTT Nord") that changed over the years.
Livorno bus network, as the entire [Regione Toscana](./Regione_Toscana "Regione Toscana"), is performed by [Autolinee Toscane](./Autolinee_Toscane "Autolinee Toscane") which manages, since 1 November 2021,[[79]](./Livorno#cite_note-79) two High Mobility Lines (*LAM Blu* and *LAM Rossa*), seventeen urban lines, one school line and six suburban routes departing from Livorno across the [Province](./Province_of_Livorno "Province of Livorno"). Autolinee Toscane operates a [funicular](./Montenero_funicular "Montenero funicular") which connect lower Montenero to the [Sanctuary](./Sanctuary_of_Montenero "Sanctuary of Montenero").[[80]](./Livorno#cite_note-80)[[81]](./Livorno#cite_note-81)

### Port

The [Port of Livorno](./Port_of_Livorno "Port of Livorno") is one of the largest seaports both in Italy and the Mediterranean Sea as a whole.
The Port has regular ferry links of the following operators with the following cities:

* [Corsica Ferries - Sardinia Ferries](./Corsica_Ferries_-_Sardinia_Ferries "Corsica Ferries - Sardinia Ferries") to [Golfo Aranci](./Golfo_Aranci "Golfo Aranci") and [Bastia](./Bastia "Bastia")
* [Grimaldi Lines](./Grimaldi_Group "Grimaldi Group") to [Barcelona](./Barcelona "Barcelona") and [Tangier](./Tangier "Tangier")
* [Moby Lines](./Moby_Lines "Moby Lines") to [Olbia](./Olbia "Olbia") and [Bastia](./Bastia "Bastia")
* [Toremar](./Toremar "Toremar") to [Capraia](./Capraia "Capraia")

### Trains

The city is served by [Livorno Centrale station](./Livorno_Centrale_railway_station "Livorno Centrale railway station").

Education
---------

### Schools

#### *Istituto Tecnico Industriale "Galileo Galilei"*

The [Industrial Technical Institute](./Secondary_education_in_Italy#Istituto_tecnico "Secondary education in Italy") named to [Galileo Galilei](./Galileo_Galilei "Galileo Galilei") was founded in 1825 as a School of Arts and Crafts in order to prepare the youngs to a profession in the sector of the mechanic industry as in the decorative arts. In 1923 the [Gentile Reform](./Gentile_Reform "Gentile Reform") transformed the school in an Industrial Technical Institute for [mechanics](./Mechanics "Mechanics") and [electrical engineering](./Electrical_engineering "Electrical engineering"), and in 1947 was added [chemistry](./Chemistry "Chemistry"). In the following years other specialities were added as [physics](./Physics "Physics"), [electronics](./Electronics "Electronics"), [biology](./Biology "Biology"), [nuclear physics](./Nuclear_physics "Nuclear physics") and [informatics](./Informatics "Informatics"). The institute is structured with 32 laboratories, 8 special school-rooms, library, film library, gymnasiums and machine-shops.[[82]](./Livorno#cite_note-82)

#### *Istituto Nautico "Alfredo Cappellini"*

The Nautical Institute Alfredo Cappellini was formed on 13 December 1863, with a Royal Law and it was the first Technical Institute in the [Province of Livorno](./Province_of_Livorno "Province of Livorno"). In 1921 it was transferred under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Navy then returned to the Ministry of Education. The school give the professional preparation to form the [Merchant navy](./Merchant_navy "Merchant navy") Officers.

#### *Liceo Classico "Niccolini Palli"*

The *[Liceo Classico](./Liceo_Classico "Liceo Classico") [Niccolini](./Giovanni_Battista_Niccolini "Giovanni Battista Niccolini")* was established on 10 March 1860 by law of [Terenzio Mamiani](./Terenzio,_Count_Mamiani_della_Rovere "Terenzio, Count Mamiani della Rovere"), then Ministry of the Public Instruction. The first *[Preside](./Dean_(education) "Dean (education)")* elected was Luigi De Steffani who remained in charge from 1862 to 1867. The Liceo was entitled to [Giovanni Battista Niccolini](./Giovanni_Battista_Niccolini "Giovanni Battista Niccolini"), [Ugo Foscolo](./Ugo_Foscolo "Ugo Foscolo")'s friend, in 1862; in 1883 it was named to [Francesco Domenico Guerrazzi](./Francesco_Domenico_Guerrazzi "Francesco Domenico Guerrazzi"); the name came into effect in 1889 and remained until the unification of the *Liceo* with the *[Istituto magistrale](./Liceo_delle_scienze_umane "Liceo delle scienze umane")*. The most famous professor was [Giovanni Pascoli](./Giovanni_Pascoli "Giovanni Pascoli") who taught [Greek](./Greek_language "Greek language") and [Latin](./Latin "Latin") from 1887 to 1895. Among the pupils were [Pietro Mascagni](./Pietro_Mascagni "Pietro Mascagni"), [Guglielmo Marconi](./Guglielmo_Marconi "Guglielmo Marconi"), [Amedeo Modigliani](./Amedeo_Modigliani "Amedeo Modigliani"), [Giosuè Borsi](./Giosuè_Borsi?action=edit&redlink=1 "Giosuè Borsi") and [Carlo Azeglio Ciampi](./Carlo_Azeglio_Ciampi "Carlo Azeglio Ciampi"), who was teacher in 1945.[[83]](./Livorno#cite_note-83)

### Library

Further information on the library: [Villa Fabbricotti](./Villa_Fabbricotti "Villa Fabbricotti")

#### Biblioteca Labronica

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Livorno_Villa_Fabbricotti_01.JPG/250px-Livorno_Villa_Fabbricotti_01.JPG)](./File:Livorno_Villa_Fabbricotti_01.JPG)

*Biblioteca Labronica F.D. Guerrazzi*

The [Biblioteca Labronica](./Biblioteca_Labronica "Biblioteca Labronica") [[it](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblioteca%20Labronica "it:Biblioteca Labronica")] on the Viale della Libertà was founded in 1816, by the fellows of the *Accademia Labronica*, which was made public in 1840 and it was given to the Comune in 1854.[[84]](./Livorno#cite_note-84)[[85]](./Livorno#cite_note-iccu-85) The civic library was dedicated to Francesco Domenico Guerrazzi in 1923[[86]](./Livorno#cite_note-86) and take place in *Villa Fabbricotti*. According to the tradition, the origin of the villa date back to the Medicean period when an edifice was built as a suburban residence for [Ferdinando II de' Medici](./Ferdinando_II_de'_Medici "Ferdinando II de' Medici"). *Villa Fabbricotti* received the name from its last owner Bernardo Fabbricotti from [Carrara](./Carrara "Carrara"), who acquired it from the English merchant Thomas Lloyd in 1881. Fabbricotti, following to adverse economic affairs, sold the Villa and the park to the [Comune](./Comune "Comune") in 1936. During World War II the building was used by the German command as headquarters, and later taken by the American forces;[[87]](./Livorno#cite_note-87) in the post-war period was restored in order to adapt it into library. In the warehouse of the *Biblioteca Labronica* are stored: 120,000 books, 1,500 [manuscripts](./Manuscript "Manuscript"), 117 [incunables](./Incunable "Incunable"), 2,000 cinquecentine (is a book printed in the 16th century) and 60,000 [autographs](./Autograph "Autograph"); the library is organized with reading rooms with 80 places of capacity, 18 seats for consultation of manuscripts, 4 internet positions and a conference room with 60 seats. The library has a collection of autographs including those of [Galileo Galilei](./Galileo_Galilei "Galileo Galilei") and [Giacomo Leopardi](./Giacomo_Leopardi "Giacomo Leopardi"), manuscripts by [Ugo Foscolo](./Ugo_Foscolo "Ugo Foscolo"), and ancient books printed in Livorno since the 17th century, including the *[Encyclopédie](./Encyclopédie "Encyclopédie")* printed in 1770 in Livorno by the ancient *Bagno dei forzati* ([Gaol](./Gaol "Gaol") of the [convicts](./Convicts "Convicts")).[[88]](./Livorno#cite_note-88)

**Omladinski fudbalski klub Grbalj** ([Serbian Cyrillic](./Serbian_Cyrillic_alphabet "Serbian Cyrillic alphabet"): Омладински фудбалски клуб Грбаљ, Serbo-Croatian pronunciation: [[gr̩̂baʎ]](./Help:IPA/Serbo-Croatian "Help:IPA/Serbo-Croatian")) is a [Montenegrin](./Montenegro "Montenegro") professional [football](./Association_football "Association football") club based in the small town of [Radanovići](./Radanovići,_Kotor "Radanovići, Kotor"), municipality of [Kotor](./Kotor "Kotor"). They currently compete in the [Montenegrin Second League](./Montenegrin_Second_League "Montenegrin Second League").

History
-------

The first football club in Radanovići, which existed only few seasons, was founded in 1970. After many years, the club was refounded in June 1995[[1]](./OFK_Grbalj#cite_note-1) and in their first season the team gained promotion to the [Montenegrin Republic League](./Montenegrin_clubs_in_Yugoslav_football_competitions_(1946–2006)#Montenegrin_Republic_League "Montenegrin clubs in Yugoslav football competitions (1946–2006)") for the 1996–97 season (third tier of the [FR Yugoslavia](./FR_Yugoslavia "FR Yugoslavia") football system). After only three seasons in the Republic League, in the summer of 1999, OFK Grbalj (*OFC Humpback*) became a member of the [FR Yugoslavia Second League](./1999–2000_Second_League_of_FR_Yugoslavia "1999–2000 Second League of FR Yugoslavia"), which was the biggest success of the team until 2006.[[2]](./OFK_Grbalj#cite_note-2) OFK Grbalj spent four seasons in the Second Yugoslav League.  
After [Montenegrin independence](./Montenegrin_independence_referendum,_2006 "Montenegrin independence referendum, 2006"), OFK Grbalj became a member of the [Montenegrin First League](./Montenegrin_First_League "Montenegrin First League"). In the 2006–07 season, the team achieved third place, just behind two of the most successful teams in national competitions, [Zeta](./FK_Zeta "FK Zeta") and [Budućnost Podgorica](./FK_Budućnost_Podgorica "FK Budućnost Podgorica"). Over the next two seasons, OFK Grbalj finished as a fourth-placed team. During subsequent seasons, the team didn't achieve the same successes as in their first seasons in top-tier competition, but they were never relegated from the First League.  
OFK Grbalj holds two all-time records in the Montenegrin First League. On 29 May 2010 they defeated [Kom](./FK_Kom "FK Kom") 11–0, which is the biggest margin of victory in the history of league. Five years later, on 23 May 2015, OFK Grbalj beat [Mornar](./FK_Mornar "FK Mornar") in [Bar](./Bar,_Montenegro "Bar, Montenegro") 7–0, which is the biggest away victory in league.  
In the 2016–17 season, OFK Grbalj had the greatest success in their history by reaching the [Montenegrin Cup final](./2016–17_Montenegrin_Cup "2016–17 Montenegrin Cup"). They lost game against [Sutjeska](./FK_Sutjeska_Nikšić "FK Sutjeska Nikšić") 1–0.  
After 14 consecutive seasons in top-tier, OFK Grbalj finished as a last-placed team in [2019-20 Montenegrin First League](./2019-20_Montenegrin_First_League "2019-20 Montenegrin First League"). After the campaign full of disappointing results, team from Radanovići was relegated to [Montenegrin Second League](./Montenegrin_Second_League "Montenegrin Second League").

Stadium
-------

Main article: [Stadion Donja Sutvara](./Stadion_Donja_Sutvara "Stadion Donja Sutvara")

OFK Grbalj play at [Stadion Donja Sutvara](./Stadion_Donja_Sutvara "Stadion Donja Sutvara"), near the main road between [Budva](./Budva "Budva") and [Kotor](./Kotor "Kotor"). Stadium capacity is 1,500 seats on one stand and it doesn't meet UEFA standards for European competitions. Except the main ground, there is a smaller artificial pitch at Donja Sutvara football complex.

Unsourced material may be challenged and removed. *(February 2021)* *([Learn how and when to remove this message](./Help:Maintenance_template_removal \"Help:Maintenance template removal\"))* |\\n\\n\\n\\nFor a chronological guide, see [Timeline of Livorno](./Timeline_of_Livorno \"Timeline of Livorno\").\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/83/Livorno_map_17th_Century.jpg/500px-Livorno_map_17th_Century.jpg)](./File:Livorno_map_17th_Century.jpg)\\n\\nFortifications of Livorno in the 17th century\\n\\n### Origins\\n\\nThe origins of Livorno are controversial, although the place was inhabited since the [Neolithic](./Neolithic \"Neolithic\") Age. This is documented by the worked bones, and pieces of copper and ceramic found on the [Livorno Hills](./Livorno_Hills \"Livorno Hills\") in a cave between Ardenza and Montenero. The [Etruscan](./Etruscan_cities \"Etruscan cities\") settlement was called Labro.[[13]](./Livorno#cite_note-13)\\n\\nThe construction of the [Via Aurelia](./Via_Aurelia \"Via Aurelia\") coincided with the occupation of the region by the [Romans](./Ancient_Rome \"Ancient Rome\"). They are also known for their [toponyms](./Toponymy \"Toponymy\") and the ruins of towers. The natural cove called Liburna is a reference to the type of ship, the [liburna](./Liburna \"Liburna\"), adopted by [Roman navy](./Roman_navy \"Roman navy\") from the [Liburnians](./Liburnians \"Liburnians\"). Other ancient toponyms include *Salviano* (Salvius) and *Antignano* (Ante ignem), which was the place situated before *Ardenza* (Ardentia), where beacons directed the ships to [Porto Pisano](./Porto_Pisano \"Porto Pisano\"). [Cicero](./Cicero \"Cicero\") mentioned Liburna in a letter to his brother, in which he called it [Labrone](./Labrone?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Labrone\").[[14]](./Livorno#cite_note-14)\\n\\n### Medieval\\n\\nLivorna is mentioned for the first time in 1017 as a small coastal village, the port and the remains of a Roman tower under the rule of [Lucca](./Lucca \"Lucca\"). In 1077, a tower was built by [Matilda of Tuscany](./Matilda_of_Tuscany \"Matilda of Tuscany\"). The [Republic of Pisa](./Republic_of_Pisa \"Republic of Pisa\") owned Livorna from 1103 and built a quadrangular fort called *Quadratura dei Pisani* (\"Quarter of the Pisans\") to defend the port.[[10]](./Livorno#cite_note-treccanilivorno-10) *Porto Pisano* was destroyed after the crushing defeat of the Pisan fleet in the [Battle of Meloria](./Battle_of_Meloria_(1284) \"Battle of Meloria (1284)\") in 1284.[[15]](./Livorno#cite_note-15)\\n\\nIn 1399, Pisa sold Livorna to the [Visconti of Milan](./Visconti_of_Milan \"Visconti of Milan\"); in 1405 it was sold to the [Republic of Genoa](./Republic_of_Genoa \"Republic of Genoa\"); and on 28 August 1421 it was bought by the [Republic of Florence](./Republic_of_Florence \"Republic of Florence\").[[10]](./Livorno#cite_note-treccanilivorno-10) The name \\'Leghorn\\' was derived from the [Genoese](./Genoese_dialect \"Genoese dialect\") name Ligorna.[[16]](./Livorno#cite_note-Ciccone-16) *Livorno* was used certainly in the eighteenth century by Florentines.[[16]](./Livorno#cite_note-Ciccone-16)\\n\\nBetween 1427 and 1429, a census counted 118 families in Livorno, including 423 persons. Monks, Jews, military personnel, and the homeless were not included in the census.[[17]](./Livorno#cite_note-17) The only remainder of medieval Livorno is a fragment of two towers and a wall, located inside the [Fortezza Vecchia](./Livorno#Fortezza_Vecchia).\\n\\n### Medicean period (1500–1650)\\n\\nAfter the arrival of the [Medici](./House_of_Medici \"House of Medici\"), the ruling dynasty of Florence, some modifications were made in the city. Between 1518 and 1534 the *[Fortezza Vecchia](./Old_Fortress,_Livorno \"Old Fortress, Livorno\")* was constructed, and the voluntary resettlement of the population to Livorno was stimulated. Livorno still remained a rather insignificant coastal fortress.[[18]](./Livorno#cite_note-18) By 1551, the population had grown to 1562 residents.[[10]](./Livorno#cite_note-treccanilivorno-10)\\n\\nSeat of the crusading and corsairing [Order of Saint Stephen](./Order_of_Saint_Stephen \"Order of Saint Stephen\") after 1561, distinctive for its aggressive approach towards the Muslim world, Livorno became a major Mediterranean [slave trade](./History_of_slavery \"History of slavery\") hub in the early modern period, rivalling Malta\\'s.[[19]](./Livorno#cite_note-19) Its share of slave population may have been over a 25% of the population.[[20]](./Livorno#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavis2018873-20)\\n\\nDuring the [Italian Renaissance](./Italian_Renaissance \"Italian Renaissance\"), when the settlement was ruled by the [Grand Duchy of Tuscany](./Grand_Duchy_of_Tuscany \"Grand Duchy of Tuscany\") of the [House of Medici](./House_of_Medici \"House of Medici\"), Livorno was designed as an \"[Ideal town](./Ideal_town \"Ideal town\")\".[[10]](./Livorno#cite_note-treccanilivorno-10) In 1577 the architect [Bernardo Buontalenti](./Bernardo_Buontalenti \"Bernardo Buontalenti\") drew up the first plan.[[10]](./Livorno#cite_note-treccanilivorno-10) The new fortified town had a [pentagonal](./Pentagonal \"Pentagonal\") design, for which it is called *[Pentagono del Buontalenti](./Livorno#Pentagono_del_Buontalenti)*, incorporating the original settlement. The *[Porto Mediceo](./Port_of_Livorno#Porto_Mediceo \"Port of Livorno\")* was overlooked and defended by [towers](./Tower \"Tower\") and fortresses leading to the [town centre](./Town_centre \"Town centre\").\\n\\nIn the late 1580s, [Ferdinando I de\\' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany](./Ferdinando_I_de\\'_Medici,_Grand_Duke_of_Tuscany \"Ferdinando I de\\' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany\"), declared Livorno a [free port](./List_of_free_ports \"List of free ports\") (*porto franco*), which meant that the goods traded here were [duty-free](./Duty-free_shop \"Duty-free shop\") within the area of the town\\'s control.\\n\\nIn 1593, the Duke\\'s administration established the *Leggi Livornine* to regulate trade.[[10]](./Livorno#cite_note-treccanilivorno-10) These laws protected merchant activities from crime and [racketeering](./Racket_(crime) \"Racket (crime)\"), and instituted laws regarding [international trade](./International_trade \"International trade\"). The laws established a well-regulated market and were in force until 1603. Also expanding Christian tolerance, the laws offered the right of public [freedom of religion](./Freedom_of_religion \"Freedom of religion\") and [amnesty](./Amnesty \"Amnesty\") to people having to gain [penance](./Penance \"Penance\") from clergy in order to conduct civil business. The Grand Duke attracted numerous Turks, Persians, Moors, Greeks, and Armenians, along with [Jewish](./Jews \"Jews\") immigrants. Sephardic Jews began to immigrate to Livorno in the late sixteenth century, following the [Alhambra Decree](./Alhambra_Decree \"Alhambra Decree\") and expulsion of Jews from Spain and Portugal. Livorno extended rights and privileges to them, and they contributed greatly to the mercantile wealth and scholarship in the city.\\n\\nLivorno became an enlightened European city and one of the most important ports of the entire [Mediterranean Basin](./Mediterranean_Basin \"Mediterranean Basin\"). Many European [foreigners](./Alien_(law) \"Alien (law)\") moved to Livorno. These included Christian Protestant reformers who supported such leaders as [Martin Luther](./Martin_Luther \"Martin Luther\"), [John Calvin](./John_Calvin \"John Calvin\"), and others. [French](./French_people \"French people\"), [Dutch](./Dutch_people \"Dutch people\"), and English arrived, along with Orthodox [Greeks](./Greeks \"Greeks\"). Meanwhile, Jews continued to trade under their previous treaties with the Grand Duke. On 19 March 1606, Ferdinando I de\\' Medici elevated Livorno to the rank of city; the ceremony was held in the *Fortezza Vecchia* Chapel of [Francis of Assisi](./Francis_of_Assisi \"Francis of Assisi\").\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/Chiesa_Santa_Caterina%2C_Livorno.jpg/250px-Chiesa_Santa_Caterina%2C_Livorno.jpg)](./File:Chiesa_Santa_Caterina,_Livorno.jpg)\\n\\n[Santa Caterina, Livorno](./Santa_Caterina_(Livorno) \"Santa Caterina (Livorno)\")\\n\\nThe [Counter-Reformation](./Counter-Reformation \"Counter-Reformation\") increased tensions among Christians; dissidents to the [Papacy](./Pope \"Pope\") were targeted by various Catholic absolute rulers. Livorno\\'s tolerance declined during the [European wars of religion](./European_wars_of_religion \"European wars of religion\"). But, in the preceding period, the merchants of Livorno had developed a series of trading networks with Protestant Europe, and the Dutch, British, and Germans worked to retain these. In 1653 a naval battle, the [Battle of Leghorn](./Battle_of_Leghorn \"Battle of Leghorn\"), was fought near Livorno during the [First Anglo-Dutch War](./First_Anglo-Dutch_War \"First Anglo-Dutch War\").\\n\\n### 17th century and later\\n\\nAt the end of the 17th century, Livorno underwent a period of great [urban planning](./Urban_planning \"Urban planning\") and expansion. Near the defensive pile of the Old Fortress, a new fortress was built, together with the town walls and the system of navigable canals through neighbourhoods. After the port of [Pisa](./Pisa \"Pisa\") had silted up in the 13th century, its distance from the sea increased and it lost its dominance in trade. Livorno took over as the main port in [Tuscany](./Tuscany \"Tuscany\"). By 1745 Livorno\\'s population had risen to 32,534.[[10]](./Livorno#cite_note-treccanilivorno-10)\\n\\nThe more successful of the European powers re-established trading houses in the region, especially the British with the [Levant Company](./Levant_Company \"Levant Company\"). In turn, the trading networks grew, and with those, Britain\\'s cultural contact with Tuscany. An increasing number of British writers, artists, philosophers, and travellers visited the area and developed the unique historical ties between the two communities. The British referred to the city in English as \"Leghorn\", derived from the Genoese term. Through the centuries, the city\\'s trade fortunes fell and rose according to the success or failure of the Great Powers. The British and their Protestant allies were important to its trade.\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/52/Livorno_map_of_the_town_%281849%29_by_Guesdon_01.jpg/330px-Livorno_map_of_the_town_%281849%29_by_Guesdon_01.jpg)](./File:Livorno_map_of_the_town_(1849)_by_Guesdon_01.jpg)\\n\\nBird\\'s-eye view of Livorno in the mid 19th century.\\n\\nDuring the [Italian campaigns of the French Revolutionary Wars](./Italian_campaigns_of_the_French_Revolutionary_Wars \"Italian campaigns of the French Revolutionary Wars\") of the late eighteenth century, Napoleon\\'s troops occupied Livorno along with the rest of Tuscany. Under the [Continental System](./Continental_System \"Continental System\"), the French prohibited trade with Britain, and the economy of Livorno suffered greatly. The French had altogether taken over Tuscany by 1808, incorporating it into the Napoleonic empire. After the [Congress of Vienna](./Congress_of_Vienna \"Congress of Vienna\"), Austrian rule replaced the French.\\n\\nIn 1861, [Italy](./Italy \"Italy\") succeeded in its [wars of unification](./Unification_of_Italy \"Unification of Italy\"). At that time the city counted 96,471 inhabitants.[[10]](./Livorno#cite_note-treccanilivorno-10) Livorno and [Tuscany](./Tuscany \"Tuscany\") became part of the new [Kingdom of Italy](./Kingdom_of_Italy \"Kingdom of Italy\") and, as part of the Kingdom, the town lost its status as a free port. The city\\'s commercial importance declined.\\n\\nIn the 18th and 19th centuries, Livorno had numerous [public parks](./Urban_park \"Urban park\") housing important museums such as the *[Museo Civico Giovanni Fattori](./Livorno#Museo_Civico_\"Giovanni_Fattori\")*, *[Museo di storia naturale del Mediterraneo](./Livorno#Museo_di_storia_naturale_del_Mediterraneo)*, and [cultural institutions](./Cultural_institution \"Cultural institution\") as the *[Biblioteca Labronica F.D. Guerrazzi](./Livorno#Biblioteca_Labronica)* and others in [Neoclassical style](./Neoclassical_architecture \"Neoclassical architecture\") as *[Cisternone](./Cisternoni_of_Livorno#La_Gran_Conserva \"Cisternoni of Livorno\")*, *Teatro Goldoni* and [Liberty style](./Liberty_style \"Liberty style\") as *Palazzo Corallo*, *[Mercato](./Market_(place) \"Market (place)\") delle Vettovaglie*, *[Stabilimento termale Acque](./Thermae \"Thermae\") della Salute*, the *[Scuole elementari](./Primary_education#Italy \"Primary education\") Benci* all the last on project by Angiolo Badaloni.\\n\\nIn the early 19th century, the American [Elizabeth Ann Seton](./Elizabeth_Ann_Seton \"Elizabeth Ann Seton\") converted from Protestantism to Catholicism while visiting Italian friends in Livorno. She later was canonized as the first American-born saint.\\n\\nDuring the 1930s, numerous [villas](./Villa \"Villa\") were built on the avenue along the sea in [Liberty style](./Art_Nouveau \"Art Nouveau\") based on designs by Cioni.[[21]](./Livorno#cite_note-21) These added to the architectural richness of the city.\\n\\nLivorno suffered extensive damage during [World War II](./World_War_II \"World War II\"). Many historic sites and buildings were destroyed by bombs of the [Allies](./Allies_of_World_War_II \"Allies of World War II\") preceding their invasion of Italy, including the [cathedral](./Livorno#Cathedral_of_Saint_Francis_of_Assisi) and [Synagogue of Livorno](./Synagogue_of_Livorno \"Synagogue of Livorno\").\\n\\nSince the late 20th century, Livorno\\'s residents have become well known for their [left-wing politics](./Left-wing_politics \"Left-wing politics\"). The [Italian Communist Party](./Italian_Communist_Party \"Italian Communist Party\") was founded in Livorno in 1921.\\n\\nClimate\\n-------\\n\\nLivorno has a hot-summer [mediterranean climate](./Mediterranean_climate \"Mediterranean climate\") ([Köppen climate classification](./Köppen_climate_classification \"Köppen climate classification\") *Csa*). Summers have warm days with the heat lingering on throughout the night, hence going above the [subtropical](./Subtropical_climate \"Subtropical climate\") threshold in spite of its relatively high latitude. Winters are mild for the latitude due to the moderating influence from the [Mediterranean Sea](./Mediterranean_Sea \"Mediterranean Sea\"). Precipitation is in a wet winter/dry summer pattern as with all climates fitting the Mediterranean definition.\\n\\nFurther information: [2017 Livorno floods](./2017_Livorno_floods \"2017 Livorno
